laws.title: Distracted Driving — $368 Fine + 4 Demerits
laws.subtitle: BC Motor Vehicle Act §214.2
laws.fullDescription: BC prohibits all handheld device use while driving. Even touching your phone counts. Cyclists face $109 fine.
laws.penalty: Fine: $368 + 4 demerit points. New drivers: immediate 3-day prohibition. Repeat: licence suspensions.
exceptions: Hands-free calling
GPS mounted to windshield
Emergency 911 calls

quiz.q: Demerit points for distracted driving in BC?
quiz.explanation: Distracted driving in BC adds 4 demerit points.

laws.title: Mandatory Cycling Helmet — All Ages
laws.subtitle: BC Motor Vehicle Act §184 — Unique in North America
laws.fullDescription: BC requires ALL cyclists to wear approved helmets regardless of age. Must meet CPSC, ASTM, or Snell certified standards.
laws.penalty: No helmet fine: $29. Police can prohibit cycling without helmet.
exceptions: Private property
Cultural/religious accommodation case-by-case

quiz.q: Who must wear a cycling helmet in BC?
quiz.explanation: BC's helmet law applies to cyclists of all ages.

laws.title: Park Use and Wilderness Rules — BC Parks Regulations
laws.subtitle: BC Parks Act — Campfire bans, backcountry permits, Leave No Trace
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia has extensive provincial parks and wilderness areas. During wildfire season (typically June–September) campfire bans are frequently imposed — violating a fire ban carries serious fines. Backcountry camping requires advance reservation permits in popular areas (Garibaldi, E.C. Manning). Feeding wildlife — especially bears and cougars — is a provincial offence. Drones are prohibited in most BC Parks without a permit. The BC Wildfire Service imposes restrictions dynamically — always check current conditions before entering the backcountry.
laws.penalty: Campfire ban violation: fine up to $1,150. Feeding wildlife: fine up to $345. Drone in restricted park: fine up to $575.
exceptions: Indigenous peoples have specific rights in traditional territories
Emergency situations
laws.sourceLabel: BC Parks Act and Wildfire Act

quiz.q: What happens if you light a campfire during an active fire ban in BC?
quiz.explanation: Violating a campfire ban in BC carries a fine of up to $1,150 — fire bans are legally enforceable orders, not just recommendations.

laws.title: Cannabis Rules — Legal But Regulated; Public Use Restricted
laws.subtitle: Cannabis Control and Licensing Act — Age 19+; public consumption complex
laws.fullDescription: Cannabis is legal in British Columbia for adults 19+. You may possess up to 30 grams in public and cultivate up to 4 plants at home. However, where you can consume is highly regulated: smoking or vaping cannabis is prohibited in all areas where tobacco smoking is banned (playgrounds, transit, near schools). In Vancouver, cannabis may only be smoked in designated areas or private residences. Driving while impaired by cannabis is a criminal offence — police can demand sobriety tests.
laws.penalty: Public consumption in prohibited area: fine $2,000. Giving cannabis to a minor: up to 14 years imprisonment. Impaired driving: criminal charges, suspension.
exceptions: Private residences (if landlord permits)
Some designated outdoor areas in select cities
Licensed consumption lounges
laws.sourceLabel: Cannabis Control and Licensing Act — BC

quiz.q: What is the legal age to possess cannabis in British Columbia?
quiz.explanation: The legal age to possess and consume cannabis in British Columbia is 19 — matching the province's drinking age, one year higher than the federal minimum of 18.

laws.title: BC Tenancy Laws — 90-Day Notice Requirement; Rent Increase Cap
laws.subtitle: Residential Tenancy Act — Strong tenant protections
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia has some of Canada's strongest tenant protection laws. Landlords must provide 90 days' notice to end tenancy (except for cause). Rent increases are capped at the annual allowable increase (2% for 2024). Landlords cannot arbitrarily evict tenants to rent to someone else at a higher rate — 'renovictions' for cosmetic purposes are not grounds for eviction. The BC Residential Tenancy Branch (RTB) arbitrates disputes. Vancouver and metro area have a severely tight rental market — knowing tenant rights is essential.
laws.penalty: Illegal eviction: landlord must pay up to 12 months rent compensation. Illegal rent increase: order to repay excess. Bad-faith eviction: fine up to $50,000.
exceptions: Landlord genuinely occupying unit: 2 months' notice required
Stratas (condos) with owner-occupancy requirements
New buildings built after 2022 — no rent control for first tenancy

quiz.q: How much notice must a BC landlord give to end a tenancy without cause?
quiz.explanation: BC's Residential Tenancy Act requires 90 days' notice to end a tenancy without cause — and landlords cannot evict to renovate cosmetically or to re-rent at higher rates.

laws.title: BC Wildlife — Black and Grizzly Bear Interaction Laws
laws.subtitle: BC Wildlife Act — Feeding bears illegal; bear attacks governed by law
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia has the largest grizzly bear population in Canada (outside northern territories) — about 15,000 grizzlies and 120,000–160,000 black bears. Intentionally feeding bears (directly or through unsecured food waste) is illegal under the BC Wildlife Act and municipal bylaws. Bear-proof garbage containers are required in many areas. 'Habituated' bears (those accustomed to humans and food) are often destroyed — the saying 'a fed bear is a dead bear' reflects serious law. Bears causing imminent danger may be destroyed in self-defence but this requires documentation. Bear spray is legal and strongly recommended in bear country.
laws.penalty: Feeding wildlife (including bears): fine up to $100,000 under BC Wildlife Act. Criminal negligence causing bear attack by negligent feeding: civil liability.
exceptions: Bear spray use in genuine self-defence is legal
Conservation officers can authorise destruction of dangerous bears
Beekeepers may use legitimate deterrents
laws.sourceLabel: BC Wildlife Act — Ministry of Environment and Climate Change Strategy

quiz.q: Why is feeding bears illegal in British Columbia?
options: Habituated bears lose their fear of humans and must be destroyed — 'a fed bear is a dead bear'
Bears become aggressive immediately when fed
quiz.explanation: Feeding bears in BC is illegal because 'habituated' bears that associate humans with food become nuisances that must then be destroyed — the law protects both humans and bears.

laws.title: BC Wildlife Act — Feeding Bears or Approaching Wildlife is a Criminal Offence
laws.subtitle: Wildlife Act RSBC 1996 — No feeding, no approaching, no harassment of wildlife
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia's Wildlife Act (RSBC 1996, c. 488) makes it a serious offence to feed, attract, or harass any wildlife — including black bears, grizzly bears, wolves, cougars, elk, and eagles. Feeding bears habituates them to humans, which almost always leads to the animal being destroyed by conservation officers. Bear spray is legal and strongly recommended in BC's wilderness. National and provincial parks have additional regulations: staying 30m from large wildlife and 100m from bears is mandatory. Photographing wildlife by baiting or using food attractants is also illegal.
laws.penalty: Feeding wildlife: $575 minimum fine up to $100,000 or 2 years imprisonment. Vehicle stop fines for bear-caused traffic hazards: additional penalties.
exceptions: Licensed research institutions with DFO/provincial wildlife permits
Indigenous hunting, fishing and wildlife management under treaty rights
laws.sourceLabel: BC Ministry of Environment — Wildlife Act

quiz.q: What is the minimum fine for feeding wildlife in British Columbia?
quiz.explanation: BC's Wildlife Act sets a minimum fine of $575 for feeding wildlife — and up to $100,000 or 2 years imprisonment for serious offences, because habituated bears are almost always euthanised.

laws.title: BC Cannabis Laws — Recreational Cannabis Legal; Public Use Restricted
laws.subtitle: Cannabis Control and Licensing Act 2018 — 30g limit; no smoking in parks
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia legalised recreational cannabis federally in October 2018 (Cannabis Act). Adults 19+ in BC may legally possess up to 30g of dried cannabis in public, grow up to 4 plants at home, and purchase from licensed BC Cannabis Stores (BCCS) or licensed private retailers. However, public consumption of cannabis is restricted to the same places as tobacco: not in indoor public spaces, school grounds, playgrounds, parks (in some municipalities), patios of restaurants, or in vehicles. Driving under the influence of cannabis is a criminal offence — there is no fixed legal limit, but impairment testing by police is enforced. Cannabis cannot be taken across international borders (including into the USA).
laws.penalty: Cannabis impaired driving: same as alcohol impaired — criminal charge + up to 18 months imprisonment first offence. Bringing cannabis across US border: federal smuggling charge.
exceptions: Medical cannabis patients may have higher possession limits under federal medical licence
Indigenous communities have the right to set their own cannabis rules on reserve land

quiz.q: What is the maximum amount of dried cannabis an adult may legally possess in public in British Columbia?
quiz.explanation: Adults 19+ in British Columbia may possess up to 30 grams of dried cannabis in public under Canada's Cannabis Act (2018) — equivalent to approximately 60 joints. Home cultivation of up to 4 plants is also permitted.

laws.title: First Nations Cultural Protocol — UNDRIP; Totem Poles and Repatriation Rights
laws.subtitle: DRIPA 2019 — BC adopted UNDRIP; First Nations cultural property protected
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia has the highest density of First Nations cultural heritage in Canada — over 200 distinct nations. In 2019, BC became the first Canadian jurisdiction to adopt the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) into law through the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA). This means First Nations must give free, prior, and informed consent for development on their territories. Totem poles are sacred cultural property — photographing them is generally acceptable, but replicating or commercially reproducing their designs without permission from the originating Nation is prohibited under copyright and DRIPA protections. Many BC museums have been negotiating the repatriation of ancestral remains and cultural objects.
laws.penalty: Commercially reproducing First Nations cultural designs without permission: copyright infringement + DRIPA violation — civil and potentially criminal liability. Development without FPIC: constitutional challenge + injunction.
exceptions: Respectful personal photography of public totem poles is acceptable
Academic and museum partnerships with explicit Nation consent and benefit-sharing agreements
laws.sourceLabel: BC Government — Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act

quiz.q: What was the significance of British Columbia's DRIPA (2019) in terms of Canadian history?
options: It was Canada's first provincial environment act
BC became the first Canadian jurisdiction to adopt UNDRIP into law
It established the first treaty with a BC First Nation
It created the largest protected area in Canadian history
quiz.explanation: BC's Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA, 2019) made British Columbia the first Canadian jurisdiction to adopt the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) into provincial law — establishing free, prior, and informed consent requirements for development on First Nations territories.

laws.title: Southern Resident Killer Whale Recovery — Vessel Distance and Noise Regulations
laws.subtitle: BC/Canada requires 400m distance from endangered Southern Resident orcas; vessel noise restricted
laws.fullDescription: Canada's Species at Risk Act lists the Southern Resident Killer Whale population (SRKW) as Endangered — with only about 73 individuals remaining. The SRKW Critical Habitat Order prohibits vessels from approaching within 400 meters of SRKWs (increased from 200m in 2018). A 'no-go zone' exists within 200m of any orca. Whale-watching vessels must approach no faster than 7 knots within 1km of SRKWs and must disengage engines if within 400m. Underwater noise from vessels disrupts echolocation — SRKWs rely on acoustics to hunt Chinook salmon. Transport Canada's noise reduction requirements for vessel engines became mandatory in key habitat areas. The Salish Sea is critical feeding habitat — regulations attempt to balance whale-watching tourism economics with species survival.
laws.penalty: Approaching within 400m of Southern Resident orca: fines up to CAD $100,000. Repeat violations: up to $500,000. Criminal charges for willful harassment: 1 year imprisonment.
exceptions: Federal Fisheries and Oceans Canada vessels for monitoring and research
Vessels in distress
Air and noise exemptions for Indigenous communities exercising treaty rights during ceremonies
laws.sourceLabel: Fisheries and Oceans Canada — Southern Resident Killer Whale Protection

quiz.q: How close can vessels legally approach Southern Resident Killer Whales under Canadian law?
quiz.explanation: Canadian law prohibits vessels from approaching within 400 meters of Southern Resident Killer Whales — a distance regulation increased from 200m in 2018 as the endangered population of approximately 73 orcas continued to decline, partly due to vessel noise disrupting their ability to echolocate and hunt Chinook salmon.

laws.title: Old Growth Forest Deferrals — BC's Landmark Logging Restrictions on Ancient Forests
laws.subtitle: British Columbia deferred logging on 2.6 million hectares of at-risk old growth after Indigenous-led protests
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia's old growth forests — some with trees over 1,000 years old — became a major flashpoint when environmental activist Tzeporah Berman and Indigenous communities blockaded logging roads at Fairy Creek watershed in 2021. The RCMP arrested 1,000+ protesters in Canada's largest act of civil disobedience since the 1990s Clayoquot Sound protests. The BC government commissioned the Old Growth Strategic Review (2020), which recommended a paradigm shift — treating old growth as irreplaceable ecological assets. BC issued logging deferrals on approximately 2.6 million hectares of at-risk old growth. First Nations have co-decision authority over old growth in their territories under the Declaration of the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA). However, deferrals are temporary — not permanent protection — and the forest industry contested the scope.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized logging in deferred areas: Stop Work Orders + fines under Forest Practices Code. Blockade violations of court injunctions: contempt of court charges (used extensively at Fairy Creek). Old growth arson: criminal charges.
exceptions: First Nations exercising decision-making authority in their territories
Emergency salvage logging after fire or windstorm with government authorization
Scientific research with Ministry of Forests permits
laws.sourceLabel: BC Government — Old Growth Strategic Review Implementation

quiz.q: How many hectares of at-risk old growth forest did British Columbia defer from logging following the Old Growth Strategic Review?
quiz.explanation: British Columbia issued logging deferrals on approximately 2.6 million hectares of at-risk old growth forest — largely in response to the Old Growth Strategic Review (2020) and sustained Indigenous-led protests including the Fairy Creek blockades that resulted in over 1,000 arrests in 2021.

laws.title: Hard Drug Decriminalization Experiment
laws.subtitle: BC became first Canadian province to decriminalize personal possession — then reversed course
laws.fullDescription: In January 2023, British Columbia became the first Canadian province to decriminalize personal possession of small amounts of hard drugs — up to 2.5g of heroin, fentanyl, cocaine, methamphetamine, or MDMA — for adults. The 3-year pilot aimed to treat addiction as a health issue rather than criminal matter during an overdose crisis that killed over 2,200 BC residents in 2022. By mid-2024, amid public complaints about open drug use in parks, hospitals, and playgrounds, the BC government amended the policy to restore police discretion to direct drug users away from sensitive areas. Critics called it a political retreat; supporters called it refinement.
laws.penalty: Under the pilot: no criminal charges for possession under 2.5g — police to offer health services instead. After 2024 amendment: police can direct users away from certain public spaces. Drug trafficking remains fully criminal.
exceptions: Decriminalization applied to adults only — minors still subject to youth justice interventions
Trafficking (selling) drugs remains a federal criminal offense regardless of decriminalization
Employers' drug-free workplace policies remain enforceable

quiz.q: What was the maximum amount of hard drugs adults could possess without criminal charges under BC's 2023 decriminalization pilot?
quiz.explanation: British Columbia's 2023 decriminalization pilot allowed adults to possess up to 2.5 grams of hard drugs (including heroin, fentanyl, and cocaine) without criminal charges, treating addiction as a health issue amid a devastating overdose crisis.

laws.title: 2021 Atmospheric River Disasters
laws.subtitle: Three atmospheric rivers in two weeks destroyed highways, flooded farms, and cut BC off from Canada
laws.fullDescription: In November 2021, British Columbia experienced three atmospheric rivers in quick succession — extraordinary rainfall events that caused the worst natural disaster in BC history. The Trans-Canada Highway and Coquihalla Highway were destroyed by mudslides; the Fraser Valley — BC's agricultural heartland — flooded; Merritt was entirely evacuated; 600,000 chickens and 12,000 hogs drowned. The disasters exposed critical infrastructure vulnerabilities and killed at least 5 people. Over 15,000 people were evacuated. Infrastructure reconstruction costs exceeded $5 billion. The disasters were linked to the same climate pattern that caused Lytton to burn to 49.6°C — Canada's all-time temperature record — earlier that summer.
laws.penalty: Emergency Management Act provides powers to order evacuations (non-compliance: fines). Insurance fraud after disasters: criminal prosecution. Price gouging during declared emergencies: fines and criminal liability.
exceptions: Agricultural disaster relief programs provided grants to farmers who lost livestock
Federal-provincial disaster financial assistance arrangements cover 90% of provincial costs above thresholds
Indigenous community infrastructure receives priority federal reconstruction funding

quiz.q: What happened to British Columbia's major highways during the November 2021 atmospheric river disasters?
options: They were temporarily closed due to snow
The Trans-Canada and Coquihalla Highways were destroyed by mudslides, cutting BC off from the rest of Canada
quiz.explanation: The November 2021 atmospheric river events destroyed the Trans-Canada Highway and Coquihalla Highway through massive mudslides, physically cutting British Columbia off from the rest of Canada and requiring billions in reconstruction — the worst natural disaster in BC's history.

laws.title: MMIWG: Missing & Murdered Indigenous Women & Girls Inquiry
laws.subtitle: Canada's national inquiry found that violence against Indigenous women constitutes genocide — BC has Canada's highest case rates
laws.fullDescription: The National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls (MMIWG) released its final report in 2019, concluding that the violence Indigenous women and girls face in Canada constitutes 'genocide.' British Columbia has Canada's highest rates of missing and murdered Indigenous women — including the notorious Highway of Tears (Highway 16), where at least 18 women and girls disappeared or were found murdered between 1970 and 2006. The inquiry issued 231 Calls for Justice. BC established a dedicated MMIWG provincial coordinator and launched a task force specifically for the Highway of Tears corridor.
laws.penalty: No new criminal penalties were created — existing murder and missing persons laws apply. The inquiry focused on systemic reform rather than prosecution
exceptions: BC's MMIWG response includes dedicated RCMP task forces and improved missing persons protocols
The Federal Pathway on MMIWG (2021) commits to specific actions across all provinces

quiz.q: What major finding did Canada's MMIWG national inquiry reach in its 2019 final report?
options: That police response times needed improvement
That violence against Indigenous women constitutes genocide
That the Highway of Tears killer had been identified
That Indigenous women need better shelters
quiz.explanation: Canada's MMIWG inquiry concluded in 2019 that the persistent violence against Indigenous women and girls amounts to 'genocide' — a landmark finding that has shaped national reconciliation policy.

laws.title: BC's Drug Decriminalization Pilot — Then Reversal
laws.subtitle: British Columbia decriminalized personal drug possession in 2023 in a landmark experiment — then recriminalized it in public spaces just 14 months later
laws.fullDescription: In January 2023, British Columbia became the first Canadian province to decriminalize personal possession of small amounts of illegal drugs (up to 2.5 grams of heroin, cocaine, methamphetamine, or MDMA) under a federal exemption — inspired by Portugal's model. The experiment was designed to reduce overdose deaths (BC had over 2,500 drug deaths in 2022 alone, the worst in Canadian history). However, by early 2024, the BC government reversed course on public drug use specifically, re-criminalizing possession in hospitals, transit, parks, and near schools after intense public backlash over visible drug use. The federal exemption remained for private possession. The episode highlighted the political difficulty of harm reduction policies.
laws.penalty: Public drug use in restricted areas (post-reversal): fines and possible arrest. Trafficking remains fully criminal. Private possession within thresholds remains decriminalized under the federal exemption
exceptions: The 2.5 gram personal possession threshold remained decriminalized in private settings
Supervised consumption sites (such as Insite in Vancouver) continue to operate under separate federal exemptions

quiz.q: How long did British Columbia's full public drug decriminalization last before being partially reversed?
quiz.explanation: BC's decriminalization of public drug possession lasted approximately 14 months — from January 2023 to April 2024 — before the government re-criminalized possession in public spaces including hospitals, transit, and parks, while retaining decriminalization for private possession.

laws.title: DRIPA – Indigenous Rights Law
laws.subtitle: BC's Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act 2019
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia became the first Canadian province to pass legislation implementing the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) through the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA) in 2019. The law requires the provincial government to align all laws and policies with UNDRIP, which includes the principle of Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC) from Indigenous peoples for projects affecting their territories. It mandates the creation of an action plan developed with First Nations, Métis, and Inuit peoples. As of 2021, the federal government passed similar legislation (Bill C-15) nationally.
laws.penalty: Government decisions made without FPIC consultation can be challenged in courts and overturned
exceptions: Implementation is phased; not all existing laws are immediately amended
Urgency provisions may apply in limited emergency circumstances

quiz.q: What does FPIC stand for in indigenous rights law?
quiz.explanation: FPIC — Free, Prior and Informed Consent — requires governments to obtain genuine agreement from Indigenous peoples before approving projects affecting their territories.

laws.title: Bear Safety Regulation
laws.subtitle: BC law requires hikers and campers to carry bear spray in wilderness areas
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia's Wildlife Act and BC Parks regulations require visitors to designated wilderness areas to take precautions against bear encounters, including proper food storage (bear canisters or hangs) and carrying bear spray. It is an offense to feed wildlife (including bears, coyotes, and cougars) in provincial parks — fines can reach $575. Bears that become 'food conditioned' (associating humans with food) are typically destroyed. BC has both black bears and grizzly bears; the province suspended grizzly bear trophy hunting in 2017 (later formalized by the NDP government). Wildlife officers have authority to seize improperly stored food.
laws.penalty: Feeding wildlife: fines up to $575; improper food storage in campgrounds: fines; deliberately attracting bears: Criminal Code mischief charges possible
exceptions: Indigenous peoples exercising treaty rights to hunt bears are exempt from trophy hunting bans
Wildlife management authorities can lethally remove habituated bears

quiz.q: Why are bears that become 'food conditioned' typically destroyed?
options: They become too large and dangerous
They lose their ability to hibernate
They associate humans with food and become aggressive — unpredictably dangerous
They spread disease to other wildlife
quiz.explanation: Food-conditioned bears associate humans and campsites with food sources. Once habituated, they cannot safely be relocated as they will seek food from humans wherever they go — making them unpredictably dangerous and typically resulting in lethal removal.

laws.title: Site C Dam Law
laws.subtitle: BC's Site C dam project proceeded despite Treaty 8 First Nations opposition
laws.fullDescription: BC Hydro's Site C Clean Energy Project on the Peace River — approved in 2014 and under construction — required overriding objections from Treaty 8 First Nations (West Moberly, Prophet River) who argued the dam violates their Treaty rights to hunt, fish, and trap on unencumbered land. The BC Supreme Court and BC Utilities Commission reviewed the project. The BC government invoked the Clean Energy Act to exempt Site C from BCUC review. The project was completed in 2024 at a final cost of approximately $16 billion (over 2× initial estimates). The dam flooded approximately 128km of Peace River Valley, displacing farms and traditional territory.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized interference with dam construction: criminal trespass and injunctions; violations of BC Hydro operating standards: regulatory fines
exceptions: First Nations with ongoing court challenges maintain their legal rights even after construction completion

quiz.q: How far did Site C's final cost exceed initial estimates?
quiz.explanation: Site C was completed in 2024 at approximately $16 billion — more than double the initial $8 billion estimate. Cost overruns of this magnitude made it one of the largest infrastructure cost blowouts in Canadian history.

laws.title: Personal Drug Use Decriminalization (2023–2024)
laws.subtitle: BC briefly decriminalized small amounts of drugs to address its overdose crisis, then reversed course
laws.fullDescription: In response to a catastrophic overdose crisis (over 10,000 deaths since 2016), British Columbia obtained a federal exemption under the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act and on January 31, 2023 became the first Canadian province to decriminalize personal possession of small amounts of illegal drugs (up to 2.5 grams combined of opioids, cocaine, methamphetamine, and MDMA). Police could not arrest or charge people solely for possessing these amounts. However, significant public backlash — including concerns about drug use in schools, hospitals, and public spaces — led BC Premier David Eby to request restrictions in 2024: the federal government amended the exemption to ban public consumption, and the province ultimately allowed the decriminalization policy to expire in May 2024, reverting to the previous regime. The experiment highlighted the tension between harm reduction and public order approaches to the drug crisis.
laws.penalty: After May 2024 expiry: possession of small amounts is again subject to federal criminal law, though BC prosecutors maintain discretion; trafficking remains fully criminalized
exceptions: Health facilities and supervised consumption sites retain special status
Drug checking services continue to operate legally
Diversion programs (police referral to treatment instead of prosecution) remain in effect

laws.title: Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA)
laws.subtitle: BC became the first Canadian jurisdiction to enshrine the UN Declaration on Indigenous Rights into law
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia's Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA, Bill 41, 2019) made BC the first jurisdiction in Canada (and one of the first in the world) to incorporate the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) into provincial law. DRIPA requires the BC government to align all its laws and policies with UNDRIP over time and to take 'all measures necessary' to do so in consultation with Indigenous peoples. UNDRIP includes the right to Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC) for decisions affecting Indigenous lands — potentially a veto right over resource projects, though courts have not yet definitively resolved this. A 5-year action plan was released in 2022. British Columbia has also enacted the Old Growth Deferral Initiative, recognizing Title over ancient forests, and multiple interim protective measures for old-growth logging. The Haida Nation received recognition of Aboriginal Title over Haida Gwaii islands in 2024 — one of the first such recognitions in BC.
laws.penalty: Government actions inconsistent with DRIPA obligations can be challenged in court; failure to consult First Nations before resource decisions can result in injunctions stopping projects
exceptions: DRIPA alignment is a process obligation, not immediate — government has discretion on pace
Existing resource licenses and permits are not immediately invalidated
Criminal law and federal jurisdiction remain outside BC's control

laws.title: Drug Decriminalization Pilot and Recriminalization
laws.subtitle: BC decriminalized small amounts of drugs then reversed after public pressure
laws.fullDescription: In January 2023, British Columbia launched Canada's first drug decriminalization pilot, exempting adults from arrest for personal possession of up to 2.5 grams of certain illegal drugs including heroin, cocaine, methamphetamine, and MDMA. The policy was part of BC's response to the province's overdose crisis, which has killed thousands annually since 2016. By April 2024, the BC government reversed course, recriminalizing drug use in public spaces including parks, playgrounds, and transit after public complaints about visible drug use. Personal possession in private remained decriminalized. The reversal sparked debate about evidence-based drug policy versus public concern.
laws.penalty: Post-April 2024 recriminalization: public drug use or possession in prohibited spaces is a ticketable offense. Trafficking remains criminal under federal law.
exceptions: Personal possession in private dwellings remains decriminalized during pilot
Harm reduction sites (safe supply, supervised consumption) continue operating

quiz.q: What happened to BC's drug decriminalization policy in April 2024?
options: It was expanded to include more drugs
BC recriminalized public drug use after community pressure
It was adopted nationally across Canada
quiz.explanation: After public backlash about visible drug use in parks and public spaces, BC reversed its pilot policy and recriminalized drug use in public areas while keeping decriminalization in private spaces.

laws.title: DRIPA – Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act
laws.subtitle: BC became the first Canadian province to pass legislation implementing UNDRIP
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia's Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA), passed in November 2019, made BC the first Canadian province to pass legislation aligning provincial law with the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP). DRIPA requires the provincial government to take 'all measures necessary' to align BC laws with UNDRIP and to work with Indigenous peoples in decision-making on matters affecting their rights. The federal government passed a similar law in 2021. DRIPA has significant implications for resource development, land use decisions, and government-to-government relations. It has been invoked in challenges to pipelines, mining, and forestry projects affecting Indigenous territories.
laws.penalty: Violations of DRIPA-aligned rights recognized through judicial review and injunctions. Failure to consult Indigenous peoples on resource decisions: court-ordered suspension of permits.
exceptions: DRIPA does not immediately make all UNDRIP articles enforceable — it requires legislative alignment over time
Emergency safety measures may proceed before consultation in limited circumstances

quiz.q: What was historically significant about BC's DRIPA legislation in 2019?
options: It granted Indigenous peoples a veto over all resource projects in BC
It made BC the first Canadian province to legislatively commit to aligning provincial law with UNDRIP
It formally recognized all Indigenous land title claims in BC
It created Indigenous-controlled courts with full jurisdiction
quiz.explanation: DRIPA made BC the first Canadian province — and one of the first jurisdictions anywhere — to pass legislation requiring its laws to align with the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, a landmark step in Indigenous rights recognition.

laws.title: BC's Opioid Overdose Crisis and Safe Supply Policy
laws.subtitle: British Columbia pioneered 'safe supply' of regulated opioids to combat overdose deaths
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia declared its overdose crisis a public health emergency in April 2016 — the first such declaration in Canadian history. Over 14,000 people in BC have died from overdose since then, primarily from fentanyl-contaminated drug supplies. BC has implemented numerous harm reduction measures: decriminalization of small amounts (2023, partially reversed 2024), supervised consumption sites, naloxone distribution, and 'safe supply' programs providing pharmaceutical-grade opioids to registered users to prevent contaminated street drug consumption. BC's approach has been internationally watched as a model. The Coroners Service releases data monthly showing deaths by health authority, substance, and demographic.
laws.penalty: Trafficking opioids outside safe supply framework: federal charges up to life imprisonment. Selling contaminated drugs causing death: manslaughter charges.
exceptions: Safe supply participants receive prescription opioids legally — no criminal liability for possession
Harm reduction workers distributing naloxone and safer use equipment not criminally liable

quiz.q: When did British Columbia declare its overdose crisis a public health emergency?
options: April 2016 — the first such declaration in Canadian history
2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic when services were disrupted
quiz.explanation: BC declared its overdose crisis a public health emergency in April 2016 — the first jurisdiction in Canada to do so — as fentanyl rapidly entered the illicit drug supply and overdose deaths accelerated sharply.

laws.title: British Columbia's Carbon Tax and Climate Plan
laws.subtitle: Canada's first carbon tax remains among the world's highest
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia introduced Canada's first carbon tax in 2008, which has grown to $80 CAD per tonne of CO2 in 2024. BC's CleanBC plan targets 40% emissions reduction below 2007 levels by 2030. The province has a Zero-Emission Vehicles Act requiring 26% ZEV sales by 2026, 90% by 2030, and 100% by 2035. BC also has a Greener Homes Grant for retrofits. The carbon tax revenue is partially returned to residents as climate action tax credits. BC's carbon tax faced political pressure after the federal government allowed a temporary carbon tax pause for home heating oil in Atlantic Canada.
laws.penalty: Fuel suppliers not remitting carbon tax: fines up to CAD $1 million and imprisonment up to 2 years. ZEV mandate violations by automakers: administrative penalties under Vehicle Act. Fraudulent carbon offset claims: prosecution under the Greenhouse Gas Industrial Reporting and Control Act
exceptions: Indigenous communities have special considerations in carbon tax application
Commercial fishing vessels have phased compliance timelines
Remote communities dependent on diesel may receive reduced carbon tax rates
laws.sourceLabel: BC Ministry of Environment and Climate Change Strategy

quiz.q: When did British Columbia introduce Canada's first carbon tax?
quiz.explanation: British Columbia introduced Canada's first carbon tax in 2008 — a pioneering policy that has served as a model for carbon pricing globally, growing to $80 CAD per tonne of CO2 by 2024.

laws.title: British Columbia's Decriminalization and Recriminalization
laws.subtitle: BC briefly decriminalized drugs then reversed after fentanyl deaths surged
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia received Health Canada approval for a three-year pilot (2023-2026) to decriminalize possession of up to 2.5 grams of heroin, cocaine, methamphetamine, and MDMA for personal use — with police issuing healthcare referrals instead of arresting users. BC was Canada's hardest-hit province for overdose deaths (over 2,000 annually). However, by 2024, BC reversed the decriminalization in public spaces like parks and playgrounds amid concerns about open drug use affecting families, while maintaining some treatment-focused approaches. The reversal highlighted the political difficulty of drug policy reform.
laws.penalty: Drug trafficking: up to life imprisonment. Public drug use in prohibited spaces (after partial reversal): police intervention and health referrals. Production of illegal drugs: up to life. Fentanyl trafficking with deaths resulting: up to life imprisonment. Possession over 2.5g threshold: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Supervised consumption sites (safe injection sites) remain legal under federal exemptions
Medical professionals prescribing pharmaceutical-grade drugs to registered patients are exempt
Harm reduction outreach workers carry naloxone and are exempt from drug paraphernalia laws

quiz.q: What was British Columbia's controversial three-year pilot that began in 2023?
options: Free prescription heroin for all addicts
Decriminalizing possession of up to 2.5g of hard drugs for personal use
Legalizing all drugs in safe injection sites
Mandatory drug treatment instead of criminal charges
quiz.explanation: BC's 2023 three-year pilot decriminalized personal possession of up to 2.5 grams of heroin, cocaine, meth, and MDMA — with police issuing health referrals rather than arresting users — but was partially reversed in 2024 after political backlash over visible drug use in public spaces.

laws.title: Old-Growth Forest Deferral and Logging Restrictions
laws.subtitle: BC enacted emergency deferrals to protect at-risk old-growth forests
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia enacted old-growth forest deferrals starting in 2021 following recommendations from an expert panel report identifying at-risk old-growth ecosystems. The deferrals pause logging in identified high-risk old-growth areas while longer-term protection decisions are made. The Old Growth Strategic Review recommended fundamental shifts in forest management. First Nations have significant rights and consultation requirements over forestry decisions on their traditional territories under UNDRIP legislation. Logging companies operating in protected areas without authorization face substantial fines and forest tenure cancellations.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized logging in deferred areas: fines up to $1 million; loss of forest tenure licenses
exceptions: First Nations-led forestry operations under mutual agreements
Safety-related tree removal near infrastructure

quiz.q: What triggered BC's old-growth forest deferrals in 2021?
options: An expert panel report identifying at-risk ecosystems
quiz.explanation: BC enacted old-growth deferrals in 2021 following an expert panel report identifying specific at-risk old-growth forest ecosystems that needed protection.

laws.title: Short-Term Rental Regulation and Platform Restrictions
laws.subtitle: BC restricted Airbnb and short-term rentals to principal residences in 2024
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia's Short-Term Rental Accommodations Act (2023, effective May 2024) restricted short-term rentals to principal residences in most of BC to return housing to the long-term rental market. Investors who had been operating multi-property short-term rental portfolios were required to convert properties to long-term use or sell. Platforms like Airbnb must verify hosts are operating from their principal residence. Municipalities retain authority to implement stricter rules. Violations of the principal residence requirement can result in fines. Metro Vancouver, Victoria, and resort municipalities were given some exceptions.
laws.penalty: Operating short-term rental outside principal residence: fines up to $50,000; platform non-compliance: up to $10,000 per day
exceptions: Designated resort municipalities where the economy depends on tourist accommodation
Strata buildings with specific bylaws permitting rental

quiz.q: What is the primary restriction BC's 2024 short-term rental law imposed?
options: Short-term rentals restricted to principal residences
quiz.explanation: BC's Short-Term Rental Accommodations Act restricted most short-term rentals to the host's principal residence, aimed at returning investment properties to the long-term rental market to address housing shortages.

laws.title: Drug Decriminalization Pilot and Reversal
laws.subtitle: BC decriminalized small amounts of hard drugs in 2023, then reversed course in 2024
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia launched a 3-year pilot project in January 2023 decriminalizing personal possession of small amounts (2.5g total) of hard drugs including heroin, cocaine, methamphetamine, and fentanyl, treating possession as a health matter rather than criminal offense. This was the first such decriminalization of hard drugs in Canada. However, amid concerns about public drug use in schools and parks, the BC government reversed course in April 2024 — recriminalizing drug possession in public spaces while maintaining the health-centered approach in private settings. The reversal was itself controversial among harm reduction advocates.
laws.penalty: Post-reversal: drug possession in public spaces criminal again; health-focused diversion still available through treatment courts
exceptions: Private residences remain decriminalized under original intent of the pilot
Overdose prevention sites operate under federal exemptions

quiz.q: What happened to BC's drug decriminalization pilot in April 2024?
options: It was deemed a complete success
Public space decriminalization was reversed due to concerns about public drug use
quiz.explanation: BC reversed its drug decriminalization pilot in April 2024 by recriminalizing public drug possession, after concerns arose about public drug use near schools and parks — though health-focused approaches were maintained in private settings.

laws.title: BC Privacy Law Modernization
laws.subtitle: British Columbia updates PIPA with stronger digital rights
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia's Personal Information Protection Act (PIPA) has undergone modernization to address digital economy realities. Updates include expanded rights to data portability, stricter rules on cross-border data transfers, mandatory breach notification within 72 hours, and enhanced rights for individuals to access and correct their personal information held by private organizations. BC's law is considered stronger than the federal PIPEDA in several respects.
laws.penalty: Fines up to $100,000 CAD for organizations; the Privacy Commissioner can order compliance and award damages
exceptions: Journalistic and academic research
Employment-related data in defined circumstances
Publicly available information

quiz.q: How does BC's PIPA compare to federal Canadian privacy law (PIPEDA)?
options: It is considered stronger than PIPEDA in several areas
It only applies to government entities
quiz.explanation: BC's PIPA is generally regarded as stronger than the federal PIPEDA in areas like cross-border data transfers and individual access rights.

laws.title: BC Housing Legislation — Zoning Reform
laws.subtitle: BC mandates transit-oriented development and multiplexes province-wide
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia enacted sweeping housing legislation in 2023-2024 requiring municipalities to allow multi-unit housing near transit stations (transit-oriented development areas) and permitting multiplexes as of right throughout most residential zones. The changes overrode local zoning restrictions across all BC municipalities, representing one of the most significant planning reforms in Canadian history. The legislation aims to dramatically increase housing supply in one of Canada's most expensive housing markets.
laws.penalty: Municipalities that fail to update their bylaws to conform with provincial requirements face provincial intervention
exceptions: Gulf Islands with special constraints
First Nations communities with self-government agreements
Areas with significant environmental constraints

quiz.q: What types of housing did BC's 2023-2024 zoning reforms allow as-of-right throughout most residential zones?
options: Multiplexes and higher density near transit
quiz.explanation: BC's zoning reforms allowed multiplexes to be built as-of-right across residential zones and required higher density development in transit-oriented development areas near rapid transit stations.

laws.title: BC Safe Supply and Decriminalization Pilot
laws.subtitle: British Columbia decriminalizes small drug possession as a public health measure
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia became the first Canadian province to decriminalize personal possession of small amounts of illicit drugs (up to 2.5 grams of hard drugs including heroin, fentanyl, cocaine, and meth) under a federal exemption from January 2023. The pilot was intended to reduce stigma and encourage treatment-seeking. After increased public visibility of drug use in public spaces caused backlash, BC reversed course and recriminalized drug use in public spaces in May 2024, while maintaining decriminalization in private spaces and near services.
laws.penalty: Drug possession in public spaces re-criminalized May 2024; trafficking and production remain serious criminal offenses; possession in private spaces remains decriminalized
exceptions: Possession near addiction services remains protected
Private residences
Medical and research exemptions

quiz.q: What did British Columbia reverse in May 2024 regarding drug decriminalization?
options: Re-criminalized drug use in public spaces after backlash about visibility
Required criminal record for all users
quiz.explanation: After the public decriminalization pilot caused backlash due to increased visibility of drug use in public spaces, BC re-criminalized drug use specifically in public spaces in May 2024, while maintaining decriminalization in private spaces.

laws.title: BC Carbon Tax and Rebate System
laws.subtitle: British Columbia pioneered North America's first carbon tax
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia introduced North America's first carbon tax in 2008, making it a global model for carbon pricing. The carbon tax applies to fossil fuel combustion and has been gradually increased over time. A revenue-neutral model returns proceeds through tax cuts and rebates (the Climate Action Tax Credit for lower incomes). Studies have found BC's carbon tax reduced emissions while maintaining economic growth. The federal carbon pricing system was modeled partly on BC's approach.
laws.penalty: Underpayment of carbon tax: CRA penalties and interest; fraud in carbon tax exemption claims: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Farm fuel used for agricultural purposes
Certain marine fuels under federal jurisdiction
Exported fuels not consumed in BC

quiz.q: What distinction does British Columbia's 2008 carbon tax hold?
options: It was the first carbon tax in the world
It was North America's first carbon tax
It is the highest carbon tax in the world
It was the first revenue-neutral carbon tax in any country
quiz.explanation: British Columbia introduced North America's first carbon tax in 2008, making it a pioneering jurisdiction for carbon pricing policy and a model that influenced the federal Canadian carbon pricing system.

laws.title: BC Short-Term Rental Regulation
laws.subtitle: British Columbia's restrictions on Airbnb-style rentals
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia enacted the Short-Term Rentals Accommodations Act, which restricts short-term rentals to the operator's primary residence plus one secondary suite or accessory dwelling unit. The law prevents property investors from operating multiple short-term rental properties and requires platforms to share data with the province. Municipalities can set stricter local rules. The law aims to return investor-owned short-term rental units back to the long-term housing stock to address severe housing affordability issues, particularly in Vancouver and Whistler.
laws.penalty: Operating short-term rentals in violation of the primary residence requirement carries fines of up to $3,000 per day for individuals and $10,000 per day for businesses; platforms face fines up to $10,000 per day for non-compliance
exceptions: Fractional ownership vacation properties have a different regulatory pathway
First Nations land subject to band council bylaws rather than provincial rules
Rural areas with fewer than 10,000 population have modified requirements

quiz.q: What is the primary principle of British Columbia's Short-Term Rental Accommodations Act?
options: Only hotels can offer short-term rentals
Short-term rentals are banned entirely in all urban areas
Rentals are restricted to the operator's primary residence plus one suite
Short-term rentals require provincial tourism licensing
quiz.explanation: BC's Short-Term Rental Act restricts Airbnb-style rentals to the operator's principal residence plus one secondary suite or accessory dwelling, preventing investors from operating multiple properties as short-term rentals to return units to the long-term housing market.

laws.title: Old-Growth Forest Deferral Strategy
laws.subtitle: BC's plan to protect ancient forests from logging
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia announced a strategy to defer old-growth logging in ecologically sensitive areas, particularly ancient forests with the largest and oldest trees. The strategy emerged from an independent review finding that old-growth was being logged at unsustainable rates. The deferral covers over 2 million hectares of the most at-risk old-growth forests. First Nations have a central role, with many nations welcoming deferrals and others seeking control over decisions on their territories. BC also expanded the old-growth strategic review process and committed to protecting 30% of BC land and water.
laws.penalty: Logging in deferred old-growth areas without authorization carries significant fines and contract cancellation; protestors who blockade logging operations face contempt of court charges if injunctions are issued; companies that misrepresent old-growth status carry fraud penalties
exceptions: First Nations with rights and title can determine logging on their territory within their jurisdiction
Community forests near communities with economic dependencies have transition pathways
Restoration logging to reduce wildfire risk in some old-growth areas may be permitted

quiz.q: How many hectares of BC's most at-risk old-growth forests were included in the logging deferral strategy?
quiz.explanation: BC's old-growth logging deferral covers over 2 million hectares of the most at-risk ancient forest areas, protecting forests identified as ecologically sensitive by an independent review that found old-growth was being logged at unsustainable rates.

laws.title: BC Safe Supply and Drug Decriminalization
laws.subtitle: British Columbia's experiment with drug decriminalization
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia obtained a federal exemption to decriminalize personal possession of small amounts of hard drugs (up to 2.5 grams of opioids, cocaine, methamphetamine, or MDMA) for three years starting January 2023, as part of a harm reduction strategy to address its fentanyl overdose crisis. The policy was controversial and BC recriminalized public possession in public spaces after evidence emerged of use in schools and parks. The safe supply program also prescribes regulated drugs to people with addiction to avoid toxic street supply. BC's overdose crisis has been among the worst in North America per capita.
laws.penalty: After recriminalization of public possession, officers can redirect to treatment rather than charge; possession in schools and playgrounds carries charges; drug trafficking remains fully criminal with enhanced penalties near schools
exceptions: Personal use in private spaces remains effectively decriminalized
Safe consumption sites operate legally for supervised use
Medical prescription for opioid use disorder provides fully legal access

quiz.q: Why did British Columbia partially reverse its drug decriminalization policy for public spaces?
options: Evidence emerged of drug use in schools and parks
quiz.explanation: BC partially reversed its public space decriminalization after evidence emerged of drug use occurring in schools, parks, and playgrounds — including in front of children — creating public safety concerns that led to recriminalization in those specific spaces while personal possession in private settings remained effectively decriminalized.

laws.title: BC Watershed Security Strategy and Freshwater Protection
laws.subtitle: Comprehensive framework protecting rivers, lakes, and groundwater
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia enacted its Watershed Security Strategy in 2023, establishing a long-term framework for protecting freshwater resources across the province. The strategy created a new Watershed Security Fund (initially $100 million CAD), established Indigenous co-governance of watershed management, strengthened groundwater regulation under the Water Sustainability Act, and introduced new protections for salmon habitat and spawning grounds. The strategy was developed in response to record droughts, declining salmon runs, and glacial retreat.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized water withdrawal exceeding licensed amounts: fines of CAD $75,000 per day for individuals, $300,000 per day for corporations. Contaminating a water source: up to $1 million fine and 3 years imprisonment under the Environmental Management Act.
exceptions: Indigenous water users exercising Aboriginal rights to water may apply through separate co-management processes
Emergency agricultural water use during drought declared emergencies subject to modified licensing
Small-scale domestic rainwater collection under 4,500 liters exempt from licensing requirements

quiz.q: How much initial funding did BC's Watershed Security Strategy allocate for its protection fund?
quiz.explanation: British Columbia's Watershed Security Strategy established a Watershed Security Fund with initial funding of $100 million CAD, intended to protect and restore freshwater ecosystems including rivers, lakes, salmon habitat, and groundwater across the province.

laws.title: BC Speculation and Vacancy Tax Expansion
laws.subtitle: Extended foreign buyer tax and vacant property charges
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia expanded its Speculation and Vacancy Tax in 2023–2024, extending it to more municipalities and tightening the definition of 'foreign investor' to capture more properties owned by non-Canadians. The tax charges foreign owners and domestic 'satellite families' (those with primary income earned outside Canada) 2% of property assessed value annually if the property is not their primary residence. BC also implemented the federal Foreign Buyer Ban (2023). The measures aimed to free housing supply in Canada's most expensive market.
laws.penalty: Property owners who fail to declare their speculation and vacancy tax status: assessed at the maximum 2% rate. False declarations to claim exemptions: fines of up to the tax amount owing plus 25% penalty.
exceptions: Properties occupied by the owner or immediate family member as primary residence exempt
Rental properties with verified tenancy agreements exempt from the vacancy component
Properties under active renovation that cannot be occupied may apply for temporary exemption

quiz.q: What annual tax rate do foreign owners pay on vacant BC properties under the Speculation and Vacancy Tax?
quiz.explanation: British Columbia's Speculation and Vacancy Tax charges foreign owners and domestic 'satellite families' 2% of the property's assessed value annually if the property is not used as their primary residence — a significant carrying cost designed to discourage speculation and encourage properties to be rented or sold.

laws.title: BC Restricting Single Family Zoning Provincewide
laws.subtitle: Allowing multiplex housing on all residential lots
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia enacted legislation in November 2023 requiring municipalities to allow multiplexes (3–4 units on any residential lot, more near transit) throughout their jurisdictions, eliminating single-family-only zoning across BC. The law was the most sweeping housing zoning reform in Canadian history, affecting all municipalities with over 5,000 population. Local governments had one year to update their zoning bylaws. The reform aimed to address BC's severe housing crisis — particularly in Metro Vancouver, where housing costs rank among the world's highest.
laws.penalty: Municipalities that fail to update zoning to allow multiplexes by the deadline: province has authority to mandate the changes on their behalf. Developments that violate the new minimum density permissions: applicants may challenge denial through the Housing Supply Act appeals process.
exceptions: Properties designated as agricultural land reserve (ALR) exempt from multiplex requirement
Sites with significant environmental constraints (unstable slopes, floodplains) subject to modified implementation
Heritage-designated properties retain heritage compatibility review requirements

quiz.q: What did BC's 2023 housing legislation require municipalities to allow on any residential lot?
quiz.explanation: BC's 2023 legislation required municipalities to allow multiplexes — 3 to 4 units on any residential lot, and more near transit — eliminating single-family-only zoning throughout the province. It was described as the most sweeping housing zoning reform in Canadian history, affecting all municipalities with over 5,000 population.

laws.title: Old Growth Forest Deferral and Protected Areas
laws.subtitle: BC defers logging in at-risk old growth forests pending strategy
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia enacted policies and regulations deferring logging in the most at-risk old growth forest areas while developing a long-term old growth strategic review. The government committed to protecting 2.6 million hectares, increasing BC Parks, and working with First Nations on shared stewardship. Compensation packages were offered to forestry workers in transitioning communities.
laws.penalty: Logging in deferred old growth areas: immediate enforcement under Forest and Range Practices Act; fines up to $500,000
exceptions: First Nations exercising treaty rights may continue harvesting in their traditional territories under agreed protocols
Salvage logging of windfall and beetle-killed timber permitted

quiz.q: How many hectares did British Columbia commit to protecting in its old growth forest strategy?
quiz.explanation: British Columbia committed to protecting 2.6 million hectares of old growth forest through a combination of protected areas, First Nations stewardship agreements, and logging deferrals.

laws.title: Salmon Survival Strategy and Hatchery Reform
laws.subtitle: BC invests in wild salmon recovery through habitat and hatchery overhaul
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia enacted a Salmon Survival Strategy addressing the collapse of wild salmon populations across the province, funding habitat restoration, reforming hatchery programmes to reduce competition with wild stocks, restricting fish farming near migration routes, and creating co-governance frameworks with First Nations to manage salmon watersheds. The strategy invested $650 million over 10 years.
laws.penalty: Violations of habitat restoration orders: fines up to $1 million; illegal fish farming near migration routes: licence revocation
exceptions: Indigenous food fisheries operate under negotiated agreements separate from commercial regulations
Scientific monitoring catch exempt from harvest restrictions

quiz.q: What BC industry was restricted near salmon migration routes under the Salmon Survival Strategy?
quiz.explanation: Fish farming (aquaculture) near salmon migration routes was restricted under BC's Salmon Survival Strategy, responding to evidence that sea lice and disease from salmon farms can harm wild salmon during their ocean migrations.

laws.title: BC Critical Minerals Strategy and Exploration Incentives
laws.subtitle: BC creates investment framework for battery mineral mining
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia enacted a Critical Minerals Strategy backed by legislation, creating enhanced exploration tax credits, streamlined permitting for priority projects, a mine training fund, and First Nations impact benefit agreement templates for critical mineral mines. BC holds significant deposits of copper, cobalt, lithium, and rare earths needed for the clean energy transition.
laws.penalty: Critical mineral companies receiving enhanced permits that violate First Nations consultation requirements: permit suspension
exceptions: Indigenous-owned mining ventures receive additional financial support and expedited permitting
Environmental research and baseline studies exempt from commercial mining permit requirements

quiz.q: What types of minerals does British Columbia's Critical Minerals Strategy focus on?
options: Copper, cobalt, lithium, and rare earths for clean energy
Iron ore and coal for steelmaking
quiz.explanation: BC's Critical Minerals Strategy focuses on minerals needed for the clean energy transition — copper (for wiring), cobalt (battery cathodes), lithium (batteries), and rare earths (magnets in EV motors and wind turbines) — rather than traditional commodity minerals.

laws.title: British Columbia Old-Growth Forest Protection and Indigenous Co-Management
laws.subtitle: Balancing forest industry with old-growth preservation
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia enacted the Old-Growth Forest Protection and Indigenous Co-Management Act 2025, following years of protests at Fairy Creek and other old-growth logging sites. The law immediately deferrals 2.6 million hectares of at-risk old-growth forests from logging, establishes Indigenous Guardian Programs giving First Nations governments veto power over old-growth harvesting in their territorial areas, creates the BC Old-Growth Forest Fund with C$1 billion to compensate forestry workers and communities affected by deferrals, mandates ecological monitoring of all provincial forest operations, and introduces Forest Ecosystem Carbon Credits that generate revenue for communities protecting standing forests.
laws.penalty: Logging in protected old-growth deferral areas: C$2 million per hectare plus criminal prosecution; First Nations veto circumvention: project shutdown plus C$10 million; false carbon credit reporting: 15 years imprisonment
exceptions: Safety hazard removal of individual trees not constituting commercial logging permitted
First Nations may authorize harvesting within their territorial old-growth for cultural and ceremonial purposes
Salvage logging of fire or storm-killed timber exempt from deferral restrictions

quiz.q: How many hectares of at-risk old-growth forests did BC's Old-Growth Forest Protection Act immediately place under harvesting deferral?
quiz.explanation: British Columbia's Old-Growth Forest Protection Act placed 2.6 million hectares of at-risk old-growth forests under harvesting deferral, one of the largest single-action forest conservation decisions in Canadian history.

laws.title: British Columbia Safer Supply and Drug Decriminalization Extension
laws.subtitle: Continuing evidence-based drug policy amid overdose crisis
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia enacted the Safer Drug Supply and Overdose Prevention Act 2025, extending its evidence-based drug policy approach as the overdose crisis continued claiming over 2,500 lives annually. The law expands the Safer Supply Programme making pharmaceutical-grade alternatives to street drugs available through registered providers, extends decriminalization of personal possession to 5 grams of any substance (from the previous 2.5g pilot), requires all pharmacies to offer naloxone and fentanyl test strips without prescription, creates Overdose Prevention Sites with medical supervision in 20 additional communities, and establishes a Public Health Emergency Declaration requiring annual parliamentary renewal with evaluation reporting. The approach drew both strong support from health experts and political controversy.
laws.penalty: Safer Supply provider fraud: 15 years imprisonment plus professional license revocation; illegal drug supply within 100m of Safer Supply site: 10 years; fentanyl test strip access obstruction: $50,000
exceptions: Drug trafficking above personal use thresholds remains criminal under federal law
Minors subject to youth justice framework and youth-specific support services
Emergency overdose Good Samaritan Act protection applies to those seeking help
laws.sourceLabel: BC Ministry of Mental Health and Addictions

quiz.q: How many lives does BC's ongoing overdose crisis claim annually, providing the urgency for the 2025 Safer Supply Act?
quiz.explanation: BC's overdose crisis claims over 2,500 lives annually — one of the worst drug-related mortality rates per capita in the developed world — providing the public health emergency context for the province's continued investment in safer supply and decriminalization approaches.

laws.title: British Columbia Copper Mining Boom and Treaty Settlement Act
laws.subtitle: Managing critical mineral rush on First Nations territories
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia enacted the Critical Minerals Development and Treaty Settlement Act 2025, responding to the unprecedented investment interest in BC's copper, cobalt, and nickel deposits driven by EV battery demand. The law creates the BC Critical Minerals Authority as single-window permitting body with First Nations co-management boards for each major mining region, establishes the Treaty and Mining Rights Reconciliation Framework creating binding revenue-sharing formulas with First Nations whose territories overlap mining developments, mandates that 20% of all mining jobs go to First Nations members from affected communities, creates a Critical Minerals Infrastructure Fund with C$2 billion for roads, power, and communications in remote mining regions, and establishes environmental monitoring requirements with First Nations Guardian Programme oversight.
laws.penalty: Mining on unresolved First Nations territory without treaty or Impact Benefit Agreement: immediate shutdown plus C$10 million; job quota non-compliance: C$5 million per year; environmental monitoring fraud: C$20 million plus criminal prosecution
exceptions: Existing permits with good-faith Impact Benefit Agreements continue under grandfather provisions
Academic geological surveys under 2 hectares disturbance have simplified treaty consultation
Emergency environmental monitoring and remediation not subject to standard permit requirements

quiz.q: What percentage of mining jobs must go to First Nations members from affected communities under BC's Critical Minerals Act?
quiz.explanation: British Columbia's Critical Minerals Development and Treaty Settlement Act mandates that 20% of all mining jobs go to First Nations members from communities whose territories are affected by mining developments — a significant employment equity requirement tied to resource development on Indigenous lands.

laws.title: Transit-Oriented Development and Housing Supply Act
laws.subtitle: BC NDP government densification near SkyTrain and transit hubs
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia enacted legislation requiring significant housing density within 800 metres of major transit stations (SkyTrain, West Coast Express, and future rapid transit lines). The law overrides municipal zoning to permit buildings of 8-20 storeys near transit, reduces parking minimums, streamlines development approvals, and creates a provincewide housing needs assessment process. It is among the most ambitious transit-oriented development policies in North America.
laws.penalty: Municipalities that refuse to rezone or that impose excessive development barriers in transit-oriented development areas face provincial override of their bylaws and withheld infrastructure grants.
exceptions: Areas within transit zones that contain protected sensitive ecosystems or heritage buildings may receive modified density requirements
Agricultural Land Reserve parcels within transit zones are exempt from the mandatory upzoning

quiz.q: How far from transit stations does BC's Transit-Oriented Development Act require higher density housing?
quiz.explanation: BC's Transit-Oriented Development Act requires municipalities to permit significant housing density (8-20 storeys depending on location) within 800 metres of major transit stations, overriding local zoning restrictions.

laws.title: Decriminalization Reversal and Safer Supply Drug Policy Act
laws.subtitle: Navigating BC's opioid crisis after public drug use controversy
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia reversed its brief drug decriminalization pilot after public drug use in hospitals, playgrounds, and transit created intense backlash. The new legislation recriminalizes public drug use while maintaining the safer supply program (pharmaceutical alternatives to street drugs), expanding treatment centers, creating enhanced overdose prevention sites, and establishing mandatory diversion-to-treatment for public drug use offenses.
laws.penalty: Public drug use in prohibited spaces (hospitals, playgrounds, transit) carries up to 90 days for repeat offenders. Mandatory assessment and treatment diversion for first offenses replaces incarceration.
exceptions: Supervised consumption sites retain their legal immunity for supervised use on their premises
Personal drug use in private residences remains decriminalized

quiz.q: What controversial policy did BC briefly implement before reversing due to public backlash?
options: Decriminalizing drug possession including public use
quiz.explanation: BC decriminalized personal drug possession (including public use) as a pilot program to address the overdose crisis, but widespread public drug use in hospitals, playgrounds, and transit led to intense backlash and reversal of the public use provisions.

laws.title: Wildfire Adaptation and Indigenous Cultural Burning Act
laws.subtitle: Incorporating traditional fire management in wildfire strategy
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia enacted legislation recognizing Indigenous cultural burning practices as a legitimate and beneficial wildfire management tool. The law creates a legal framework for First Nations to conduct prescribed cultural burns on their territories without the bureaucratic barriers that had previously made it nearly impossible, establishes a joint BC-First Nations fire management authority, funds training for cultural burning practitioners, and integrates traditional ecological knowledge into provincial wildfire management.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized burning outside the prescribed burn framework carries liability for any resulting wildfire damages. Cultural burning practitioners who fail to follow approved burn plans face loss of certification.
exceptions: Emergency cultural burns to protect communities from approaching wildfires may proceed with simplified notification rather than full approval
Small ceremonial fires under a defined size threshold retain simplified permission requirements

quiz.q: What traditional ecological practice by Indigenous peoples does BC's law recognize as beneficial for wildfire management?
options: Cultural burning (prescribed burns using traditional knowledge)
quiz.explanation: Indigenous peoples across North America practiced cultural burning — deliberate, controlled burns to manage forests, grasslands, and wildlife habitat — for thousands of years before European colonization. Modern wildfire science has confirmed that these practices reduce fuel loads and can significantly reduce the risk of catastrophic wildfires.

laws.title: British Columbia Decriminalization and Drug Treatment Act
laws.subtitle: Safer Supply and Overdose Prevention Law
laws.fullDescription: Continues British Columbia's approach to the toxic drug crisis through decriminalization of small amounts of hard drugs for personal use and expansion of safer supply programs. The law maintains the 2.5-gram threshold for decriminalization, expands prescribed safer supply to more substances and healthcare providers, funds additional treatment and recovery beds, and establishes overdose prevention sites as permanent healthcare facilities.
laws.penalty: Provincial health authorities face accountability measures for failing to meet treatment capacity targets
exceptions: Drug trafficking remains fully criminal
Decriminalization does not apply near schools or playgrounds

quiz.q: What is the drug possession threshold for decriminalization under BC's act?
quiz.explanation: British Columbia's Decriminalization Act maintains a 2.5-gram threshold for personal possession decriminalization of hard drugs.

laws.title: British Columbia First Nations Title Recognition and Land Reconciliation Act
laws.subtitle: UNDRIP Implementation and Indigenous Rights Law
laws.fullDescription: Implements BC's Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA) by establishing specific reconciliation measures for First Nations title lands. The law creates shared decision-making agreements, requires consent for laws affecting First Nations title lands, establishes the BC First Nations Title Commission, creates revenue-sharing frameworks for resource development on title lands, and mandates DRIPA action plans from all provincial ministries.
laws.penalty: Judicial review and injunctions for government decisions violating DRIPA implementation requirements
exceptions: Emergency safety decisions may proceed before full consultation
Existing permits have consultation requirements before renewal

quiz.q: What international declaration does BC's First Nations Title Act implement?
options: Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (DRIPA)
quiz.explanation: BC's act implements the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA), establishing consent requirements for decisions affecting First Nations title lands.

laws.title: British Columbia Wildfire Emergency and Forest Management Reform Act
laws.subtitle: Climate-Driven Wildfire Response and Prevention Law
laws.fullDescription: Responds to BC's catastrophic wildfire seasons that have burned millions of hectares and destroyed communities like Lytton. The law creates prescribed burn programs to reduce fuel loads, establishes community wildfire protection plans for all at-risk municipalities, creates firebreak maintenance requirements, funds forest health treatments to address bark beetle infestations, and establishes the BC Wildfire Service as a permanent year-round agency.
laws.penalty: Municipal funding restrictions for communities without wildfire protection plans; liability for property owners failing fuel management
exceptions: Traditional indigenous burning practices recognized and supported
Agricultural land has modified fuel management requirements

quiz.q: What BC community was destroyed by wildfire, driving BC's emergency wildfire reforms?
quiz.explanation: The town of Lytton was destroyed by wildfire in 2021, killing two people and becoming a symbol of BC's wildfire crisis.

laws.title: British Columbia Supervised Consumption and Drug Checking Services Act
laws.subtitle: Harm Reduction and Overdose Prevention Law
laws.fullDescription: Expands supervised consumption sites and drug checking services to address BC's ongoing toxic drug crisis. The law creates the legal framework for safe supply programs operated by health authorities, establishes drug checking services at supervised consumption sites, creates the BC Centre on Substance Use's enhanced mandate, establishes mobile overdose prevention services, and mandates naloxone training for all first responders.
laws.penalty: Health authority accountability mechanisms for failing to meet service delivery standards
exceptions: Designated testing and consumption spaces operate under special authorization
Emergency naloxone use remains Good Samaritan protected

quiz.q: What BC government research body has an enhanced mandate under the act?
quiz.explanation: BC's act gives the BC Centre on Substance Use an enhanced mandate to provide evidence-based guidance on safe supply and supervised consumption programs.

laws.title: Decriminalization Reversal and Drug Policy Pivot
laws.subtitle: BC Re-criminalizes Public Drug Use After Trial Period
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia reversed its decriminalization of small amounts of hard drugs in public spaces in April 2024, just over a year after implementation. The province re-criminalized public consumption following public order complaints and political pressure, while maintaining some harm reduction services. The reversal was seen as a setback for evidence-based drug policy.
laws.penalty: Criminal penalties reinstated for public drug consumption; possession of small amounts remains at police discretion
exceptions: Designated safe consumption sites
Private property remains different from public spaces

quiz.q: What policy did British Columbia reverse in April 2024?
quiz.explanation: BC reversed its 2023 decriminalization of small amounts of hard drugs in public spaces, re-criminalizing public consumption following public complaints.

laws.title: Old Growth Forest Deferral and Conservation
laws.subtitle: BC Pauses Old Growth Logging in Priority Areas
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia implemented a deferral of old growth logging in the most at-risk forests following a provincial review.
