The government worked with First Nations to develop long-term conservation agreements. Environmental groups argued the deferrals were insufficient while the forestry industry sought certainty about long-term timber supply.
laws.penalty: Logging violations in deferred areas subject to enforcement
exceptions: First Nations-approved cultural harvesting
Existing operational commitments winding down

quiz.q: What triggered BC's old growth logging deferrals?
options: Provincial old growth review recommending protection of at-risk forests
quiz.explanation: BC's old growth deferrals followed a provincial old growth review that recommended deferring logging in the most at-risk forests while conservation agreements were developed.

laws.title: Wildfire Preparedness and Community Resilience
laws.subtitle: BC Addresses Increasing Wildfire Frequency
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia enacted comprehensive wildfire preparedness legislation following devastating fire seasons including the 2023 fires that destroyed the town of Lytton and threatened Kelowna. The law required defensible space around properties, updated building codes for fire-resistant construction, and expanded the wildfire management budget.
laws.penalty: Property compliance orders; fines for non-compliant defensible space
exceptions: Heritage buildings given adaptation time
Agricultural land different standards

quiz.q: What BC town was destroyed by wildfire in a major 2023 disaster?
quiz.explanation: The town of Lytton, BC was largely destroyed by a wildfire in 2021, and the 2023 fires threatened Kelowna, driving comprehensive wildfire preparedness legislation.

laws.title: Gig Worker Rights and App-Based Driver Protections
laws.subtitle: BC Establishes Minimum Protections for Platform Workers
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia enacted legislation establishing minimum earnings, expenses coverage, and accident insurance for app-based ride-hailing and delivery workers. The law stopped short of employee classification but created a third category with some protections. Uber and Lyft opposed the measures while worker advocates called for more.
laws.penalty: Platform company fines for non-compliance
exceptions: Driver cooperative platforms different treatment
Part-time threshold provisions

quiz.q: What type of workers did BC's legislation establish minimum protections for?
quiz.explanation: British Columbia established minimum protections for app-based ride-hailing and delivery workers including minimum earnings, expenses coverage, and accident insurance.

laws.title: Short-Term Rental Restrictions and Airbnb Regulation
laws.subtitle: BC Reins in Vacation Rental Platforms
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia enacted legislation restricting short-term rentals to principal residences, pulling thousands of units back to long-term rental market. The law targeted investors using multiple properties as Airbnbs rather than providing housing. Other BC municipalities including Vancouver implemented stricter enforcement.
laws.penalty: Fines up to $50,000 per day for non-compliant STR operators
exceptions: Principal residence exemption
Designated resort municipalities

quiz.q: What did BC's short-term rental law restrict Airbnb to?
quiz.explanation: BC restricted short-term rentals to principal residences only, targeting investors using multiple properties as Airbnbs at the expense of long-term housing availability.

laws.title: Old-Growth Forest Protection and Indigenous Rights
laws.subtitle: BC defers logging on ancient forests following Indigenous pressure
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia contains 75% of Canada's remaining old-growth forests. Indigenous communities, environmental groups, and scientists pressured the government to protect ancient trees. BC implemented old-growth deferrals — temporary logging bans on high-risk old-growth areas. The First Nations Major Agreement requires consent from Indigenous title holders. The province faces tensions between timber industry jobs and irreplaceable ecosystem protection. Some First Nations support logging for economic development, others oppose it on cultural grounds.
laws.penalty: Logging in deferred old-growth areas is suspended pending strategic review
exceptions: First Nations with proper title can make determinations about their traditional territories
Safety removals for road clearing or fire management continue in deferred areas

laws.title: Zoning Reform and Housing Supply Push
laws.subtitle: BC overrides single-family zoning to allow density across the province
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia passed sweeping zoning reform legislation allowing small-scale multi-unit housing province-wide — overriding single-family zoning in all municipalities. The legislation requires transit-oriented development density near major transit stations. BC's housing affordability crisis, especially in Metro Vancouver, has made housing the dominant political issue. The reforms are among North America's most ambitious attempts to end exclusionary single-family-only zoning. The government also regulated short-term rentals to return units to long-term housing.
laws.penalty: Municipalities must update bylaws to comply with provincial zoning override within specified timelines
exceptions: Agricultural land reserve land protected from residential rezoning
Heritage-designated properties have modified density rules preserving historic character

laws.title: Wildfire Season Expansion and Emergency Management
laws.subtitle: BC's wildfire seasons grow longer, larger, and more destructive
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia's wildfire seasons have expanded dramatically — 2023 saw over 2.8 million hectares burned, the largest in BC history. Fires forced evacuation of Kelowna (200,000 people) and threatened communities across the Interior. Climate change, beetle-killed forests, and decades of fire suppression creating fuel accumulations all contribute. BC has expanded prescribed burning, forest thinning, and community FireSmart programs. The province deploys thousands of firefighters and aerial resources but cannot match the scale of fires.
laws.penalty: Burning restrictions during high-risk periods carry fines; failure to report fires carries criminal liability
exceptions: Indigenous communities can conduct cultural burning with appropriate notification and safety planning
Agricultural burning for pest control has specific windows and approval process

quiz.q: How much area burned in British Columbia's record 2023 wildfire season?
quiz.explanation: BC's 2023 wildfire season burned over 2.8 million hectares — the largest in provincial history — forcing evacuation of Kelowna and other communities and exceeding firefighting capacity.

laws.title: Old-Growth Forest Protection and Logging Industry Transition
laws.subtitle: British Columbia balancing forest conservation with timber economy
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia is home to some of the world's last old-growth temperate rainforest, including ancient cedar, Douglas fir, and Sitka spruce trees thousands of years old. Environmental groups and Indigenous nations have pushed for protection of remaining old-growth stands, while the logging industry — a major employer in rural BC — argues that sustainable forestry practices make some harvesting compatible with conservation. The BC government has implemented the Old Growth Strategic Review and deferred logging in some high-priority old-growth areas, but environmental groups argue the deferrals are insufficient and enforcement is weak. The Fairy Creek blockade in 2021 was one of Canada's largest acts of civil disobedience, with over 1,000 arrests of people blocking logging roads. Indigenous title and treaty rights over traditional territories where old-growth exists create additional legal complexity. BC's forests also face severe pressure from climate change-driven wildfires, mountain pine beetle infestations, and drought.
laws.penalty: Logging without proper permits or in deferred areas carries fines and license consequences; blockaders faced contempt of court charges
exceptions: First Nations have rights to timber on their territories that operate under different frameworks

quiz.q: What was significant about the Fairy Creek blockade in British Columbia in 2021?
options: It stopped a major pipeline construction
It was one of Canada's largest acts of civil disobedience with over 1,000 arrests
It resulted in the permanent protection of all old-growth forests
It was the first blockade to win an Indigenous land title case
quiz.explanation: The Fairy Creek blockade in 2021 became one of Canada's largest acts of civil disobedience, with over 1,000 arrests of protesters blocking logging roads to protect old-growth forest from harvesting.

laws.title: LNG Export Ambitions and Indigenous Consent Battles
laws.subtitle: British Columbia pursuing liquefied natural gas while navigating Indigenous rights
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia has significant natural gas reserves in its northeast and has pursued LNG (liquefied natural gas) export infrastructure to access Asian markets through Pacific Gateway terminals. The LNG Canada project — a joint venture including Shell, Petronas, and others — is constructing a major export terminal at Kitimat on BC's coast. The Trans Mountain Pipeline expansion, which carries Alberta oil sands products to the BC coast for export, was completed in 2024 after years of delays and Indigenous rights battles. BC's LNG ambitions intersect with complex Indigenous rights — many proposed pipeline routes cross unceded First Nations territories. Courts have required consultation and consent processes that have both slowed projects and given Indigenous communities negotiating leverage. BC's LNG exports would increase Canada's greenhouse gas emissions significantly, creating tension with federal climate commitments.
laws.penalty: Energy projects require provincial and federal permits, environmental assessments, and Indigenous consultation; court-ordered injunctions have stopped pipeline construction when rights are violated
exceptions: Existing infrastructure has different regulatory requirements than new construction

quiz.q: Where is the LNG Canada export terminal being constructed in British Columbia?
quiz.explanation: LNG Canada is constructing a major liquefied natural gas export terminal at Kitimat on British Columbia's northern coast, designed to export Canadian natural gas to Asian markets through Pacific shipping routes.

laws.title: Atmospheric Rivers and Flooding Climate Disaster
laws.subtitle: British Columbia experiencing unprecedented weather extremes
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia experienced a series of catastrophic climate-related disasters in 2021 that killed hundreds and caused billions in damage. The 2021 heat dome — an unprecedented atmospheric event — killed over 600 people in a province unaccustomed to extreme heat, with temperatures reaching 49.6°C (121°F) in Lytton before the town was destroyed by wildfire the next day. Atmospheric river events in November 2021 caused catastrophic flooding in the Fraser Valley, cutting off Highway 1 (BC's main highway) and devastating agricultural communities and infrastructure. BC has since recognized climate change as a crisis requiring adaptation, investing in heat response systems (cooling centers, air conditioning for vulnerable residents), flood infrastructure, and wildfire management. The events represent a new reality for a province that had considered itself relatively climate-safe.
laws.penalty: Building codes are being updated for heat and flood resilience; municipal emergency management carries legal obligations
exceptions: Heritage buildings may receive modified requirements

quiz.q: What temperature record was set in Lytton, BC during the 2021 heat dome?
quiz.explanation: Lytton, BC reached 49.6°C (121°F) during the 2021 heat dome — Canada's all-time temperature record — before the town was destroyed by wildfire the following day, exemplifying the compound climate disasters that struck BC in 2021.

laws.title: NDP Minority and Conservative Surge
laws.subtitle: BC politics shift rightward as cost of living crisis dominates
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia's October 2024 election produced a razor-thin NDP minority government under David Eby, with the Conservative Party of BC under John Rustad surging dramatically. The Conservatives had been a fringe party but capitalized on cost-of-living concerns, housing affordability and discontent with NDP drug decriminalization policies. BC's experiment with decriminalizing small amounts of illegal drugs was partly reversed under public pressure. The minority NDP government required Green Party support to govern.
laws.penalty: Drug decriminalization policy modified to exclude public spaces after public pressure
exceptions: Harm reduction services continue operating
Overdose prevention sites maintain legal status

quiz.q: What BC policy was partly reversed under public pressure during the 2024 election period?
quiz.explanation: BC's drug decriminalization policy, which had allowed possession of small amounts of illegal drugs, was partly reversed under public pressure to exclude public spaces like parks and transit, becoming a major election issue.

laws.title: Old Growth Forest Protection Deferral
laws.subtitle: BC government delays logging of endangered ancient forests
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia committed to protecting 2.6 million hectares of old-growth forest through a deferral process following recommendations from a government-commissioned report warning of ecosystem collapse. However implementation has been slow and contentious, with logging companies challenging deferrals, Indigenous nations asserting rights over their territories' old-growth forests and enforcement gaps criticized by environmental groups. BC's old-growth forests represent some of the largest trees in North America and irreplaceable biodiversity.
laws.penalty: Logging in deferred old-growth areas requires ministerial approval; violations face forestry permit cancellation
exceptions: Indigenous-led economic forestry in their territories has different regulatory path
Beetle-killed standing trees sometimes excluded from strictest protections

quiz.q: How many hectares of old-growth forest did BC commit to protecting through its deferral process?
quiz.explanation: BC committed to protecting 2.6 million hectares of old-growth forest through a deferral process following a government-commissioned report warning of ecosystem collapse if logging of ancient forests continued.

laws.title: Opioid Crisis and Decriminalization Experiment
laws.subtitle: BC responds to record overdose deaths with unprecedented policy
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia has experienced Canada's worst opioid overdose crisis, with thousands dying annually from fentanyl-contaminated drug supplies. BC implemented a three-year experiment decriminalizing small amounts of hard drugs for personal use, becoming the first Canadian province to do so. However public disorder concerns—people consuming drugs openly in parks and public spaces—prompted the province to walk back decriminalization in public spaces while maintaining it in private. The crisis has forced fundamental questioning of drug enforcement versus health approaches.
laws.penalty: Decriminalization removed criminal penalties for small amounts; public consumption in certain spaces re-criminalized under amendments
exceptions: Safe injection sites and overdose prevention sites maintain legal operations
Medical-grade safe supply programs operate under Health Canada authorization

quiz.q: What made BC's approach to hard drugs unique in Canada from 2023?
options: Decriminalization of small amounts for personal use
quiz.explanation: BC became the first Canadian province to decriminalize small amounts of hard drugs for personal use, though it later walked back decriminalization in public spaces due to concerns about open drug use in parks and transit—a contentious experiment in responding to record overdose deaths.

laws.title: BC Carbon Tax
laws.subtitle: North America's First Carbon Price
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia introduced North America's first comprehensive carbon tax in 2008 under a liberal government, taxing all fossil fuels burned in the province. The revenue-neutral tax started at $10/tonne and rose to $65/tonne by 2024, with revenue returned to residents via income tax cuts and rebates. BC's carbon tax is widely studied as a policy success, demonstrating that carbon pricing can reduce emissions without harming economic growth. The province also has a Low Carbon Fuel Standard for transportation fuels.
laws.penalty: Tax evasion on carbon tax: substantial fines and back-taxes; same penalties as income tax evasion
exceptions: Fuels exported out of BC
Fuels used in international aviation/shipping
Indigenous traditional activities

laws.title: BC Safer Supply Drug Policy
laws.subtitle: North America's Progressive Drug Approach
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia declared a public health emergency over opioid deaths in 2016 — Canada's first such declaration. BC has pioneered 'safer supply' programs providing pharmaceutical-grade opioids to people with severe addiction, reducing overdose deaths. In 2023, BC decriminalized possession of small amounts of illegal drugs for personal use (up to 2.5g), making it the first Canadian province to do so, though BC recriminalized public use in 2024 after complaints about visible drug use. BC also has extensive overdose prevention sites and naloxone distribution.
laws.penalty: Drug trafficking still criminal; decriminalized possession (personal amounts) for adults; public consumption recriminalized in 2024
exceptions: Youth under 18 not covered by adult decriminalization
Public settings where recriminalized

laws.title: BC Employment Standards and Workers Compensation
laws.subtitle: Strong Protections on the Pacific Coast
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia's Employment Standards Act and Workers Compensation Act provide comprehensive worker protections. BC has a $17.40/hour minimum wage (2024) and strong protections for temporary foreign workers and domestic workers. WorkSafeBC, BC's workers' compensation board, provides no-fault compensation for work injuries and is internationally recognized for its occupational safety programs. BC also pioneered equal pay legislation and pay transparency — employers with 1,000+ employees must publish pay ranges in job postings and annual pay gap reports. BC's agricultural workers gain access to collective bargaining rights.
laws.penalty: WorkSafeBC: claims compensation; employer safety violations: significant fines and prosecution; pay equity violations: human rights tribunal
exceptions: Some owner-operators may be self-insured
Federally regulated workers under Canada Labour Code

laws.title: BC Free Post-Secondary and Childcare
laws.subtitle: Canada's Most Progressive Education Province
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia participates in the federal $10/day childcare program and has among Canada's strongest post-secondary access programs. UBC (University of British Columbia) and SFU (Simon Fraser University) are globally ranked research universities. BC invested heavily in reconciliation with Indigenous peoples — UNDRIP implementation affected education through Indigenous language revitalization programs and mandatory Indigenous education content in K-12 curriculum. BC also piloted 'discovery-based' math curriculum (later modified after criticism) and has progressive sex education curriculum.
laws.penalty: Teacher certification through the BC College of Educators; school standards enforced by Ministry; childcare licensing required
exceptions: Independent schools receive partial public funding under certain conditions
First Nations can establish their own schools under self-governance agreements

laws.title: BC Provincial Nominee Program
laws.subtitle: British Columbia's tech and trades immigration pathways
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia's Provincial Nominee Program (BC PNP) selects immigrants for skills in tech (Tech Pilot stream), healthcare, trades, and other priority sectors. BC has become a major destination for Chinese and South Asian immigrants. Vancouver has the highest proportion of visible minorities of any Canadian city. BC also provides services to temporary foreign workers and has advocated for increased immigration levels to address housing construction labor shortages. BC's Immigration Act establishes the provincial framework within Canada's shared federal-provincial immigration system.
laws.penalty: Employers exploiting temporary foreign workers face BC Employment Standards Act penalties; fraudulent credential representations to BC PNP lead to inadmissibility findings at federal level
exceptions: Seasonal agricultural workers have dedicated federal stream
International graduates from BC institutions may apply under BC PNP international graduate stream

quiz.q: British Columbia's BC PNP Tech Pilot stream is specifically designed to attract workers in which sector?
quiz.explanation: BC's Tech Pilot stream within the Provincial Nominee Program fast-tracks immigration for workers in over 30 tech occupations including software engineers, computer scientists, and IT professionals, reflecting Vancouver's growing tech industry.

laws.title: BC Drug Decriminalization Pilot
laws.subtitle: British Columbia's experimental drug decriminalization
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia implemented a Health Canada-approved drug decriminalization pilot (January 2023 – January 2026) — the first in Canada — allowing adults to possess up to 2.5g of illicit drugs (heroin, cocaine, methamphetamine, MDMA, fentanyl) without criminal charges. This was a public health response to BC's catastrophic opioid overdose crisis (2,500+ deaths annually). The pilot was controversial: government re-criminalized use in public spaces after disorder concerns (2024). BC declared the overdose crisis a public health emergency in 2016 — the first province to do so.
laws.penalty: During pilot (2023-2026): possession under 2.5g is no longer criminal (health referral instead); possession over 2.5g remains criminal; trafficking remains a serious crime; public consumption was re-criminalized by amendment in 2024
exceptions: Decriminalization pilot covers adults 18+
The 2.5g threshold is cumulative across substance types
Safe supply programs provide pharmaceutical-grade opioids to prevent fentanyl deaths
laws.sourceLabel: BC Drug Decriminalization Pilot and Overdose Emergency

quiz.q: British Columbia's drug decriminalization pilot allows possession of up to how much illicit drugs without criminal charges?
quiz.explanation: BC's Health Canada-approved decriminalization pilot (2023-2026) allows adults to possess up to 2.5 grams of illicit drugs (heroin, cocaine, meth, MDMA, fentanyl) without criminal charges, instead receiving a health referral — as a response to 2,500+ annual overdose deaths.

laws.title: BC Human Rights Code LGBTQ+ Protections
laws.subtitle: British Columbia's LGBTQ+ rights framework
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia's Human Rights Code protects against discrimination based on sexual orientation (added 1992) and gender identity/expression (added 2016). BC has been progressive on LGBTQ+ rights, with Vancouver Pride being one of North America's largest. BC law requires school districts to have LGBTQ+-inclusive policies. BC provides legal recognition for non-binary gender markers on provincial documents. The BC Human Rights Tribunal adjudicates LGBTQ+ complaints. BC has seen high-profile cases involving LGBTQ+ conversion practices.
laws.penalty: LGBTQ+ discrimination: BC Human Rights Tribunal remedies including compensatory damages and systemic remedies; conversion therapy on minors: prohibited under federal law (Criminal Code amendment 2022); hate crimes: federal Criminal Code enhanced penalties
exceptions: Religious organizations have some exemptions for employment in religious roles
Aboriginal organizations have some community-specific exemptions
laws.sourceLabel: BC Human Rights Tribunal LGBTQ+ Protections

quiz.q: Canada's federal prohibition on conversion therapy was enacted through what legislative mechanism in 2022?
options: Criminal Code amendment banning conversion therapy practices
quiz.explanation: Canada amended the Criminal Code in January 2022 to prohibit conversion therapy — making it a criminal offense to perform conversion therapy on anyone, to cause someone to undergo it, to advertise it, or to receive financial benefit from it. The maximum sentence is 5 years imprisonment.

laws.title: Press Freedom and Anti-SLAPP Protections
laws.subtitle: British Columbia has strong press protections including BC's Protection of Public Participation Act
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia enacted the Protection of Public Participation Act in 2019, one of Canada's strongest anti-SLAPP laws, protecting journalists and public speakers from meritless defamation and nuisance suits. BC journalists benefit from federal source protection and provincial court recognition of reporter privilege. Vancouver is a significant media market with the Vancouver Sun, Globe and Mail offices, and CBC BC. BC has strong freedom of information laws under the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act. Journalists covering natural resources, Indigenous issues, and politics are particularly active.
laws.penalty: Anti-SLAPP law allows early dismissal with costs against plaintiffs; reporter privilege protects sources
exceptions: Applicants can overcome SLAPP dismissal by showing substantial merit

quiz.q: What does British Columbia's Protection of Public Participation Act (2019) protect journalists from?
options: Meritless lawsuits intended to silence reporting (SLAPPs)
quiz.explanation: BC's Protection of Public Participation Act (2019) is an anti-SLAPP law that protects journalists and public speakers from meritless lawsuits (Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation) filed to silence reporting, allowing early dismissal with cost awards.

laws.title: BC's PIPA and Digital Rights Protections
laws.subtitle: British Columbia has its own private sector privacy law governing social media data
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia has its own private sector privacy law, the Personal Information Protection Act (PIPA), which governs how organizations collect, use, and disclose personal information — including data collected through social media. BC's Information and Privacy Commissioner (OIPC) has been active in investigating social media platforms. BC has been involved in pan-Canadian investigations into Facebook and other platforms. The OIPC issued findings on TikTok's data practices. BC residents have both federal PIPEDA protections (for federally regulated activities) and PIPA for provincially regulated activities.
laws.penalty: PIPA violations: OIPC can order compliance; fines available for serious violations
exceptions: PIPEDA applies to federally regulated activities; PIPA governs provincial activities

quiz.q: What unique feature of British Columbia's privacy framework distinguishes it from most Canadian provinces?
options: Its own private sector privacy law (PIPA) separate from federal PIPEDA
quiz.explanation: British Columbia (along with Alberta and Quebec) has its own private sector privacy legislation (PIPA) substantially similar to PIPEDA, meaning BC residents are protected by both federal and provincial privacy laws depending on the context — giving BC's OIPC jurisdiction over many social media privacy complaints.

laws.title: BC's Money Laundering Crisis and Financial Regulation
laws.subtitle: British Columbia was the center of Canada's massive 'Vancouver Model' money laundering scandal
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia became the center of Canada's most significant money laundering scandal — the 'Vancouver Model' where billions in drug cartel proceeds were laundered through BC real estate, casinos, and luxury car dealerships throughout the 2010s. BC's Cullen Commission (2022) documented systemic failures allowing organized crime to launder tens of billions. The BC Financial Services Authority (BCFSA) oversees financial institutions provincially. BC implemented new anti-money laundering reporting requirements for real estate professionals. BC's casino regulator BCLC has been reformed. The scandal exposed gaps in Canada's federal anti-money laundering framework.
laws.penalty: BCFSA regulatory enforcement; new AML requirements for real estate professionals; ongoing investigations
exceptions: Federal FINTRAC has primary jurisdiction over AML enforcement

quiz.q: What was the 'Vancouver Model' of money laundering documented by BC's Cullen Commission?
options: A scheme laundering drug cartel proceeds through BC real estate, casinos, and car dealerships
quiz.explanation: The 'Vancouver Model' was a sophisticated money laundering scheme in which billions in drug cartel proceeds (particularly from fentanyl trafficking) were laundered through British Columbia's real estate market, casinos, and luxury car dealerships — documented by the Cullen Commission (2022) as a systemic failure involving billions annually.

laws.title: BC Food Safety Act & FoodSafe Certification Requirements
laws.subtitle: British Columbia requires mandatory food safety certification and licenses all food establishments
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia's Food Safety Act requires all food premises to be licensed and meet provincial food safety standards. BC uniquely requires that all food service establishments have at least one person with FoodSafe Level 1 certification (a food safety training program) present during all hours of operation — a more stringent requirement than many other provinces. The BC Centre for Disease Control (BCCDC) monitors foodborne illness outbreaks and provides guidance. BC has specific rules for its significant aquaculture and seafood industry — BC is a major salmon producer and has strict handling and labeling rules for seafood products. BC's Food Premises Regulation covers everything from temperature control to pest management.
laws.penalty: Operating without food premise license: fines up to $3,000 per day; operating without FoodSafe-certified person on duty: can contribute to closure order; critical violations: immediate closure until corrected
exceptions: Private farms selling direct to consumers have agricultural exemptions
Traditional Indigenous food gathering and sharing has modified application of provincial rules
Temporary market vendors with event permits have simplified processes

quiz.q: What unique staffing requirement does BC's Food Safety Act impose on all food service establishments?
options: A licensed dietitian must approve all menus
At least one FoodSafe Level 1 certified person must be present during all hours of operation
All food handlers must have university-level food science training
A government food inspector must be on-site weekly
quiz.explanation: BC requires that all licensed food premises have at least one person with FoodSafe Level 1 certification present during all operating hours — ensuring a trained food safety person is always on-site, not just that someone in the organization has the certification.

laws.title: BC Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act and BCSPCA Powers
laws.subtitle: BC SPCA holds unique statutory enforcement authority
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia's Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act (PCAA) gives the BC SPCA unique statutory authority to enforce animal cruelty laws — unlike most provinces, the BC SPCA's Special Constables have full police powers for animal welfare enforcement. The PCAA prohibits causing or permitting unnecessary suffering, requires adequate food, water, shelter, and care, and allows seizure of animals at risk. BC also has specific regulations for commercial dog breeding facilities (Dog Breeders Regulation) and requires licensing. Exotic animal ownership is restricted in many BC municipalities. The province also has the Livestock Brand Act for farm animal identification.
laws.penalty: Summary conviction: up to $75,000 fine and 24 months imprisonment; indictable offence: up to 5 years; prohibition on owning animals for life in serious cases
exceptions: Normal farm practices under the Farm Practices Protection Act
Licensed hunting and trapping
Research under CCAC protocols
Standard veterinary procedures
laws.sourceLabel: BC Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act

quiz.q: What makes the BC SPCA's animal welfare enforcement role unusual compared to most other Canadian provinces?
options: It is funded by the federal government
BC SPCA officers have no enforcement powers at all
BC SPCA Special Constables hold statutory police powers for animal welfare enforcement
The BC SPCA reports to the RCMP
quiz.explanation: Unlike most Canadian provinces, the BC SPCA's Special Constables are granted full police powers under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act — giving a private charity statutory enforcement authority, a unique arrangement in Canadian law.

laws.title: BC Family Law Act — Guardianship and Property Division
laws.subtitle: BC's 2013 Family Law Act replaced custody with guardianship
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia's Family Law Act (2013) modernized BC family law significantly. It replaced 'custody' with 'guardianship' for parents and introduced 'parenting time' and 'parenting responsibilities.' BC uses the 'equal division' approach for family property — all property acquired during the relationship divided equally unless significantly unfair. Notably, BC's Act also covers unmarried (common-law) couples who have lived together for 2 years — giving them property rights similar to married spouses. This is more expansive than many provinces. BC family law covers same-sex couples equally. Protection orders for domestic violence are available through the Act.
laws.penalty: Family law enforcement through BC Supreme Court and Provincial Court; support enforcement by Family Maintenance Enforcement Program (FMEP); contempt for violations
exceptions: Excluded property: pre-relationship property, gifts, inheritances
Family agreements (prenuptial/cohabitation) can modify rights
Short-term relationships may have different property rules
laws.sourceLabel: BC Family Law Act, SBC 2011 c 25

quiz.q: What expanded right does BC's Family Law Act give to unmarried couples who live together?
options: Common-law couples who've lived together 2+ years get property rights similar to married spouses
Common-law couples can get divorce certificates
Cohabiting couples are treated as legally married after 6 months
quiz.explanation: BC's Family Law Act extends property division rights to unmarried (common-law) couples who have lived together for at least 2 years — giving them the right to equal division of family property acquired during the relationship, similar to married spouses. This is more generous than many Canadian provinces.

laws.title: BC Residential Tenancy Act & Rent Increase Limits
laws.subtitle: CPI-capped rent increases and strong tenant protections
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia's Residential Tenancy Act governs landlord-tenant relations. Since 2018, annual rent increases are capped at the rate of inflation (CPI only). The BC Residential Tenancy Branch (RTB) resolves disputes. Landlords must give three months' notice for owner-occupancy evictions and pay one month's rent as compensation. The province introduced the Home Owner Grant to reduce property taxes on primary residences, and the Speculation and Vacancy Tax targets empty homes in major urban areas.
laws.penalty: Illegal rent increases: tenants entitled to full reimbursement; landlord faces up to $50,000 penalties
exceptions: Rent increase cap tied to CPI annually
Three months notice plus one month compensation for owner-occupancy evictions

quiz.q: What compensation must BC landlords pay when evicting for owner-occupancy?
quiz.explanation: BC law requires landlords to provide three months' written notice AND pay the tenant one month's rent as compensation when evicting for owner-occupancy, one of Canada's strongest protections against owner-move-in evictions.

laws.title: BC Business Practices and Consumer Protection Act
laws.subtitle: Comprehensive consumer rights and unfair practices law
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia's Business Practices and Consumer Protection Act (BPCPA, 2004) is one of Canada's most comprehensive consumer protection laws. It prohibits deceptive and unconscionable acts in consumer transactions. Consumers have a right to dispute unauthorized charges on credit cards. The Direct Sales Cancellation Act gives consumers 10 days to cancel direct sales contracts. BC's specific protections include the Homeowner Protection Act for new home buyers, the Debt Collection Industry Act, and the Credit Reporting Act. BC's Consumer Protection BC (formerly FICOM) regulates payday lenders, bailiffs, and travel agents. The law allows class actions for consumer protection violations.
laws.penalty: BPCPA violation: consumer can cancel contract and recover all payments; AG enforcement with fines up to $100,000
exceptions: 10-day cancellation right for direct sales
Class actions permitted for consumer protection violations
laws.source: Business Practices and Consumer Protection Act SBC 2004
laws.sourceLabel: BC Business Practices Consumer Protection Act

quiz.q: What type of credit card protection does BC's BPCPA provide consumers?
options: Right to dispute unauthorized charges on credit cards
Government guarantee of all credit card purchases
quiz.explanation: BC's BPCPA gives consumers the right to dispute unauthorized charges on their credit cards, requiring card issuers to reverse the charges pending investigation — an important protection against fraudulent transactions and unauthorized subscription charges.

laws.title: BC Speculation & Vacancy Tax
laws.subtitle: BC SVT — 2% for foreign owners, 0.5% for Canadians
laws.fullDescription: British Columbia's Speculation and Vacancy Tax (SVT) applies to residential properties in major BC cities left vacant or used by foreign owners/satellite families. Rates: 2% for foreign owners/untaxed worldwide income, 1% for other Canadians, 0.5% for BC residents. Owners must declare status annually. Revenue funds affordable housing.
laws.penalty: Failing to declare: 2% default rate applied. Tax evasion: penalties and reassessment.
exceptions: Primary residences exempt
Properties actively rented (at least 6 months/year) exempt
New construction exempt for first year
Strata/condo bylaws preventing rental may exempt from SVT

quiz.q: What is the BC Speculation and Vacancy Tax rate for foreign owners?
quiz.explanation: BC's Speculation and Vacancy Tax charges foreign owners and those with untaxed worldwide income a 2% annual tax on the assessed value of vacant or underutilized BC residential property, aimed at reducing housing speculation.

laws.title: BC Human Rights Code — Discrimination Protections
laws.subtitle: BC Human Rights Code — Multiple protected grounds
laws.fullDescription: BC's Human Rights Code prohibits discrimination in employment, tenancy, services, and publications based on race, colour, ancestry, place of origin, religion, marital status, family status, physical or mental disability, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, and age. BC has a Human Rights Commissioner and Tribunal.
laws.penalty: Discrimination findings: remedies include compensation, policy changes, orders to cease discrimination.
exceptions: Special programs benefiting disadvantaged groups permitted
Religious organizations have some hiring exemptions
BFOR (Bona Fide Occupational Requirement) defense

quiz.q: What body adjudicates human rights complaints in British Columbia?
quiz.explanation: The BC Human Rights Tribunal is an independent administrative tribunal that adjudicates human rights complaints under BC's Human Rights Code, covering discrimination in employment, tenancy, and services.

laws.title: Site C Dam — Controversial $16 Billion Project
laws.subtitle: BC Hydro Site C — Peace River hydroelectric
laws.fullDescription: Site C is a controversial 1,100 MW hydroelectric dam on the Peace River, costing $16 billion (original estimate $8.8 billion). Completed in 2025, it will generate electricity for 450,000 homes. Treaty 8 First Nations opposed the project as a treaty violation. The BC Utilities Commission raised concerns about project economics. It remains among Canada's most debated infrastructure projects.
laws.penalty: N/A — infrastructure project. Environmental violations during construction carry fines.
exceptions: Treaty 8 Nations have ongoing litigation about treaty rights
Environmental assessment conditions must be met
BC Hydro rates will increase to cover costs

quiz.q: Which First Nations group most prominently opposed the Site C dam as a treaty rights violation?
quiz.explanation: Treaty 8 First Nations (West Moberly, Prophet River, and others) have been the most prominent opponents of Site C, arguing that flooding their traditional Peace River valley lands violates the 1899 Treaty 8 and their rights.

laws.title: BC Safe Supply & Drug Decriminalization
laws.subtitle: BC Decriminalization (2023) — Personal use of drugs
laws.fullDescription: BC was the first Canadian province to receive a federal exemption to decriminalize personal possession of small amounts of illicit drugs (2023–2026 trial). Adults 18+ may possess up to 2.5g total of opioids, cocaine, meth, or MDMA for personal use without criminal charges. The policy aims to reduce stigma and treat addiction as a health issue.
laws.penalty: Over 2.5g total: still criminal charges. Trafficking remains illegal regardless.
exceptions: Children under 18 still face youth criminal justice responses
Possession in certain public spaces (near schools, playgrounds) restricted
2026 sunset: program may be extended or modified
laws.sourceLabel: BC Ministry of Mental Health and Addictions

quiz.q: How much combined illicit drugs can an adult possess under BC's decriminalization policy?
quiz.explanation: Under BC's drug decriminalization trial (2023–2026), adults 18+ may possess up to 2.5 grams total of illicit drugs (opioids, cocaine, methamphetamine, MDMA) for personal use without criminal charges.

laws.title: Wild Salmon Policy & Pacific Salmon Treaty
laws.subtitle: BC Wild Salmon Policy — Conservation priority
laws.fullDescription: BC's Wild Salmon Policy (2005) establishes conservation as the top priority for Pacific salmon management, with harvest only when conservation objectives are met. BC and the federal government share jurisdiction. The Pacific Salmon Treaty (US-Canada) governs transboundary stocks. Wild salmon runs have declined dramatically due to climate change, habitat loss, and aquaculture.
laws.penalty: Fishing without license or in closed areas: federal Fisheries Act charges, fines.
exceptions: Indigenous food, social, and ceremonial (FSC) fishing rights recognized
Commercial and sport fisheries open when runs allow
Hatchery fish on some runs supplement wild stocks
laws.sourceLabel: DFO Pacific Region — Wild Salmon Policy

quiz.q: What is the top priority established in BC's Wild Salmon Policy?
quiz.explanation: BC's Wild Salmon Policy explicitly establishes conservation as the top priority for wild salmon management — harvest (commercial, sport, and ceremonial) is only allowed when conservation objectives are met.

laws.title: BC Foreign Buyer Tax — Additional Property Transfer Tax
laws.subtitle: BC FPTX — 20% additional PTT for foreign buyers
laws.fullDescription: BC added a 20% Additional Property Transfer Tax (FPTX) on residential property purchased by foreign nationals or foreign-controlled corporations in Metro Vancouver, Fraser Valley, Capital Regional District, and other areas. The tax was increased from 15% to 20% in 2018. Combined with federal foreign buyer rules, BC has significantly restricted foreign residential investment.
laws.penalty: Misrepresentation to avoid FPTX: 100% of tax avoided plus 10% penalty.
exceptions: Canadian citizens and PRs exempt
Work permit holders in BC for 1+ year may qualify for exemption
Refugee claimants exempt

quiz.q: What is the BC Foreign Buyer Tax rate on residential property in designated regions?
quiz.explanation: BC's Additional Property Transfer Tax (FPTX) for foreign buyers in designated areas (Metro Vancouver, etc.) is 20%, raised from 15% in 2018. This is in addition to the standard Property Transfer Tax.

laws.title: BC Declaration on Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA)
laws.subtitle: BC DRIPA (2019) — First in Canada to adopt UNDRIP
laws.fullDescription: BC became the first Canadian province to adopt the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) into provincial law in 2019. DRIPA requires BC to bring provincial laws into alignment with UNDRIP over time and calls for free, prior, and informed consent for major decisions affecting Indigenous peoples. Implementation is ongoing.
laws.penalty: N/A directly — framework law requiring alignment of other laws.
exceptions: Implementation occurs through negotiated agreements and law review
Not every UNDRIP provision immediately changes existing law
Federal jurisdiction limits BC's ability to fully implement

quiz.q: What was significant about BC's DRIPA (2019) in the Canadian context?
options: It gave First Nations full provincial authority
It was the first provincial law to adopt UNDRIP in Canada
It banned resource development on treaty lands
It established the BC First Nations government
quiz.explanation: BC's Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA) was the first law by any Canadian province to formally adopt the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP), committing BC to align its laws with UNDRIP.

laws.title: TransLink — Metro Vancouver Transit Authority
laws.subtitle: South Coast BC Transportation Authority — Integrated transit
laws.fullDescription: TransLink operates Metro Vancouver's integrated transit network: SkyTrain, buses, SeaBus, West Coast Express commuter rail, and manages major roads and bridges. TransLink is governed by a regional board. The Compass Card integrates all services. SkyTrain is largely automated and driverless. The Broadway extension and other expansions are planned.
laws.penalty: Fare evasion: $173 fine. Assault of transit staff: criminal charges.
exceptions: HandyDART service for those with disabilities
Concessional fares for seniors, students, children
Monthly passes at reduced per-trip cost

quiz.q: What automated transit technology does Metro Vancouver's SkyTrain primarily use?
quiz.explanation: SkyTrain in Metro Vancouver is primarily a driverless automated light rapid transit (ALRT/MALRT) system — one of the longest driverless urban transit networks in the world.

laws.title: BC Employer Health Tax — Replacing MSP Premiums
laws.subtitle: BC EHT (2019) — Payroll-based health funding
laws.fullDescription: BC replaced individual Medical Services Plan (MSP) premiums with an Employer Health Tax (EHT) in 2019. The EHT is paid by employers at 1.95% of BC payroll for payrolls over $1.5 million (partial credit for smaller). The elimination of MSP premiums (previously ~$900/year per adult) was a significant benefit to BC residents.
laws.penalty: Non-payment of EHT: interest, penalties, CRA-style enforcement.
exceptions: Charities and non-profits: lower rates and higher exemption threshold
Payrolls under $500,000: exempt
Public sector bodies have phased implementation

quiz.q: What did BC's Employer Health Tax (2019) replace?
quiz.explanation: BC replaced individual MSP (Medical Services Plan) premiums with the Employer Health Tax (EHT) in 2019. This shifted health funding from individuals (who previously paid ~$900/year per adult) to employers based on payroll.

laws.title: BC Rental Housing — Landlord-Tenant Act
laws.subtitle: BC Residential Tenancy Act — Strong tenant protections
laws.fullDescription: BC's Residential Tenancy Act provides strong tenant protections. Rent increases limited to the annual provincial allowance (tied to inflation, max 3% in 2024 for most units). No renovictions (renovation evictions) without proper process. Landlords must have one of 17 specific reasons to end tenancy. The Residential Tenancy Branch adjudicates disputes.
laws.penalty: Illegal rent increase: repayment order. Wrongful eviction: 12 months' rent.
exceptions: Manufactured home parks have separate legislation
Co-operative housing has different rules
Owner-occupied properties with 2 or fewer rental suites have some variations

quiz.q: What is the maximum BC residential rent increase allowed for most tenancies in 2024?
quiz.explanation: BC's 2024 rent increase guideline is 3% for most residential tenancies, based on the provincial inflation formula. Landlords cannot increase rent above this amount without Residential Tenancy Branch approval.

laws.title: Wildlife Act — BC Grizzly Bear Hunt Ban
laws.subtitle: BC Wildlife Act — Grizzly trophy hunt ended 2017
laws.fullDescription: BC banned the trophy hunting of grizzly bears in 2017, ending a controversial hunt that had been a major point of conflict with First Nations. First Nations had long opposed the trophy hunt as incompatible with their relationship with the bear. Limited First Nations ceremonial and subsistence hunting continues. BC has about 15,000 grizzly bears.
laws.penalty: Illegal grizzly trophy hunting: up to $100,000 fine, license revocation.
exceptions: First Nations ceremonial and subsistence hunting maintained
Self-defense or public safety kills permitted with immediate reporting
Bear management kills authorized by BC Conservation Officer Service

quiz.q: Why did BC ban grizzly bear trophy hunting in 2017?
options: Strong First Nations opposition and changing public values
quiz.explanation: BC's grizzly trophy hunt ban (2017) was driven primarily by First Nations opposition — many nations consider the grizzly sacred and had long opposed trophy hunting — combined with shifting BC public values against killing wildlife for trophies.

laws.title: Forestry & Old-Growth Logging Controversy
laws.subtitle: BC Old Growth Strategic Review — Complex provincial issue
laws.fullDescription: BC's forestry sector employs tens of thousands and is central to the economy. Old-growth logging (trees 250+ years old) is controversial — protesters have blocked logging roads at Fairy Creek (2021 — largest act of civil disobedience in BC history). BC's Old Growth Strategic Review (2021) recommended deferring logging in high-risk old growth. Implementation is ongoing and contested.
laws.penalty: Protesters violating injunctions at logging sites: fines, arrest for contempt of court.
exceptions: First Nations may have unique arrangements about old-growth on their territories
Some old-growth protected in parks
Sustainable forestry certification allows some old-growth harvest with conditions

quiz.q: What site became the center of Canada's largest civil disobedience protest in 2021?
quiz.explanation: Fairy Creek on Vancouver Island became the center of BC's largest civil disobedience action in 2021, when thousands of protesters blockaded logging roads to prevent old-growth logging. Over 1,000 arrests were made — the largest in Canadian history.

laws.title: BC ICBC — Public Auto Insurance Monopoly
laws.subtitle: Insurance Corporation of BC — Mandatory public auto insurance
laws.fullDescription: BC has a public auto insurance monopoly through ICBC (Insurance Corporation of BC). All BC drivers must buy basic auto insurance from ICBC. Enhanced/additional coverage available from private insurers. BC moved to a no-fault Enhanced Care model in 2021, replacing tort-based claims with treatment-focused benefits. ICBC premiums are based on driving record, not credit score.
laws.penalty: Driving without ICBC basic insurance: vehicle impound, fine up to $598.
exceptions: Motorized bicycles and some specialty vehicles have different requirements
Farming vehicles on farm property may have exemptions
Off-highway vehicles have separate ICBC coverage options

quiz.q: What major change to BC's auto insurance system occurred in 2021?
options: Switch to no-fault Enhanced Care model replacing tort-based claims
quiz.explanation: BC's ICBC switched to a 'no-fault' Enhanced Care model in May 2021, replacing the previous tort-based (litigation) system. Injured parties now receive treatment benefits directly rather than suing at-fault drivers.

laws.title: BC Pharmacare & PharmaCare Programs
laws.subtitle: BC PharmaCare — Prescription drug coverage
laws.fullDescription: BC PharmaCare provides income-based prescription drug coverage to BC residents. The Fair PharmaCare plan has deductibles and copays based on household income. Seniors get enhanced coverage through Plan B. BC has worked toward universal pharmacare but full implementation awaits the federal Canada Pharmacare program rollout.
laws.penalty: N/A — benefit program.
exceptions: Income determines deductible levels
Catastrophic Drug Program helps those with very high drug costs
Some drugs on BC's drug benefit list, others require Special Authority review

quiz.q: Under BC's Fair PharmaCare, what determines a household's annual deductible for prescription drug coverage?
quiz.explanation: BC's Fair PharmaCare sets annual deductibles based on household income — lower-income households have lower deductibles, while higher-income households pay more before PharmaCare coverage kicks in.

laws.title: BC CleanBC Plan — Carbon Tax & Net Zero
laws.subtitle: BC Carbon Tax — First in North America (2008)
laws.fullDescription: BC introduced North America's first revenue-neutral carbon tax in 2008, starting at $10/tonne and rising annually. The CleanBC plan (2018) set a goal of net-zero by 2050 and 40% emissions reduction by 2030. BC's carbon tax is now aligned with the federal carbon price ($65/tonne in 2024, rising to $170/tonne by 2030). BC has significant LNG development tension with climate goals.
laws.penalty: Carbon tax is embedded in fuel prices — not a direct penalty. Large emitters face separate trading requirements.
exceptions: Carbon tax exemptions for some agricultural fuels
First Nations using gasoline for certain activities may qualify for relief
Natural gas used in export LNG facilities has complex treatment

quiz.q: When did British Columbia introduce North America's first carbon tax?
quiz.explanation: British Columbia introduced North America's first revenue-neutral carbon tax in July 2008, starting at $10/tonne of CO2. The tax was revenue-neutral initially, with equivalent income and business tax reductions.

laws.title: Pacific Salmon Farm Transition — DFO Decision
laws.subtitle: BC Atlantic salmon farm phase-out
laws.fullDescription: Following a Federal Court ruling and DFO reviews, BC is transitioning away from open-net salmon farming in the Discovery Islands area (near wild salmon migration routes). The federal government has ordered some salmon farms to close. The industry is under pressure to transition to closed-containment systems. BC's salmon farming is a $500M+ industry employing thousands.
laws.penalty: Operating farms without valid federal licenses: closure orders, fines.
exceptions: Closed-containment facilities may continue with appropriate approvals
Transition funding provided to affected workers
Some areas outside key migration routes may retain licenses longer
laws.sourceLabel: Fisheries and Oceans Canada — Salmon Aquaculture

quiz.q: Why is BC transitioning away from open-net salmon farming near the Discovery Islands?
options: Proximity to wild salmon migration routes and concerns about disease/sea lice spread
quiz.explanation: Open-net salmon farms in the Discovery Islands sit directly on critical wild salmon migration routes. Studies linked sea lice from farms to juvenile wild salmon mortality. Federal Court and DFO ordered closures to protect endangered wild salmon runs.

laws.title: BC Judicial Council & Court System
laws.subtitle: BC Supreme Court, Court of Appeal, and Provincial Court
laws.fullDescription: BC's court system has three tiers: BC Provincial Court (lower-level criminal, family, small claims up to $35,000, civil to $35,000), BC Supreme Court (serious criminal, civil matters), and BC Court of Appeal. BC's small claims process ($35,000 limit, raised in 2024) is accessible without lawyers. Supreme Court civil matters now increasingly use Case Planning Conferences.
laws.penalty: Contempt of court: fines or imprisonment.
exceptions: Small claims: no lawyers typically, maximum $35,000
Family law: duty counsel available at many courthouses
Specialized courts: mental health court, Indigenous court, drug treatment court

quiz.q: What is the maximum claim amount in BC's Small Claims Court (as of 2024)?
quiz.explanation: BC's Small Claims Court has a maximum claim of $35,000 (raised in 2024), providing accessible dispute resolution for smaller amounts without requiring lawyers — though parties may bring legal representation.

laws.title: BC Education — School System & BC Graduation Program
laws.subtitle: BC K-12 Education — Provincial curriculum
laws.fullDescription: BC's school system is governed by the Ministry of Education and Child Care. Public schools are tuition-free for K–12. BC's New Curriculum (2016) emphasizes competencies over content, including critical thinking, communication, and creative thinking. The BC Graduation Program requires completion of 80 credits (including provincial literacy and numeracy assessments). French Immersion widely available.
laws.penalty: Truancy: parents may face bylaw violations in some districts.
exceptions: Home learning (distance education) offered through DL schools
Independent schools operate with varying degrees of Ministry funding
On-reserve schools may follow First Nations education authorities

quiz.q: How many credits must BC students earn to graduate under the BC Graduation Program?
quiz.explanation: BC's Graduation Program requires students to earn 80 credits, including required courses in English, Social Studies, Mathematics, Science, and Career Education, plus provincial literacy and numeracy assessments.

laws.title: BC Short-Term Rental Act (2024) — Airbnb Restrictions
laws.subtitle: BC Short-Term Rental Accommodations Act
laws.fullDescription: BC's Short-Term Rental Accommodations Act (2024) restricts short-term rentals (Airbnb, VRBO) to the principal residence of the host in most BC municipalities. Secondary suites and laneway homes may be used as STRs if it's the owner's principal residence. This applies in BC communities with 10,000+ population. The aim is to return STR units to the long-term rental market.
laws.penalty: Operating non-compliant STR: up to $3,000/day fine. Platforms listing prohibited STRs: fines up to $10,000/day.
exceptions: Resort municipalities and some tourist areas may have different rules
Strata buildings retain right to ban STRs
Rural communities under 10,000 population have more flexibility

quiz.q: Under BC's Short-Term Rental Act (2024), what is the primary restriction on Airbnb-style rentals?
options: Must register and pay hotel tax
Limited to principal residence of the host
quiz.explanation: BC's 2024 Short-Term Rental Accommodations Act restricts STRs in most municipalities to the principal residence of the host — you cannot list a second home, investment property, or secondary suite you don't live in as a short-term rental.

laws.title: BC Coastal Zone Management — Fisheries & Oceans
laws.subtitle: BC coastal regulations — Marine protected areas
laws.fullDescription: BC's Pacific coast has 27,000 km of coastline with significant marine biodiversity. Federal and provincial rules govern fishing, shipping, and coastal development. Pacific Rim National Park Reserve and other marine protected areas limit fishing and development. BC's oceans strategy is jointly managed with DFO. The Great Bear Rainforest Agreement protects 6.4 million acres of coastal temperate rainforest.
laws.penalty: Fishing in marine protected areas: federal Fisheries Act charges, fines.
exceptions: First Nations food and ceremonial fishing rights in protected areas
Scientific research with DFO permits
Traditional Indigenous stewardship activities recognized
laws.sourceLabel: BC Ministry of Land, Water and Resource Stewardship

quiz.q: How many kilometers of coastline does BC's Pacific coast have?
quiz.explanation: BC has approximately 27,000 km of coastline — one of the longest in the world — including the mainland coast and thousands of islands. This extensive coastline requires comprehensive federal-provincial ocean management.
